📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ford’s return to the top class of the 24 Hours of Le Mans was finally unveiled during the Thanksgiving Day NFL game between the Detroit Lions and Chicago Bears, along with an official name that clearly evokes the manufacturer’s past success: GT41.

According to recent reports, of course, there weren’t 39 cars before the GT40, as that name comes from the fact that the car was 40 inches tall. The GT41, for what it’s worth is 41 inches tall… almost. Technically, the car is 41.7 inches from the ground to the top of its air intake, a dimension dictated by the current FIA regulations for the LMDh class. But GT42 doesn’t quite have the same ring to it.

And while the GT41 is based off the same Oreca chassis as used by the Genesis GMR-001 and outgoing Alpine A424 and Acura ARX-06, the car and team is a wholly internal Ford effort. “Everything that we’re building, it’s in-house,” remarked Mark Rushbrook, global director of Ford Racing, “It's the design, the engineering, the development, all the technical elements of the car.”.

According to recent reports, that internal approach particularly applies to the engine, which Rushbrook calls the heart of the car. The naturally aspirated 5.4-liter V-8 is based off Ford’s production engines, so much so that the block is shared with the supercharged 5.2-liter in the Mustang Dark Horse SC and F-150 Raptor R and is pulled straight from the line at the Essex Engine Plant in Windsor, Ontario. Assembled inside Ford’s dyno lab at the tech giant’s headquarters in Dearborn, Michigan, every part inside the racing engine “is designed by a Ford engineer,” according to Joseph Hendrickson, motorsports powertrain calibration engineer. “The engines are also tested on a dynamometer inside the same building. It’s a huge point of pride for us,” he remarked.

The final livery of the GT41 that will race at Le Mans will be revealed closer to the start of the 2027 WEC calendar, which being at Qatar in March. The car seen here features a camouflage pattern made of the Ford Racing wordmark, with Easter eggs hidden throughout that reflect the team’s pride as an American and Detroit-based automaker; look closely, and you’ll see an American flag, a bald eagle head, the Statue of Liberty, the Spirit of Detroit, and a football.

Until then, testing of the GT41 continues at several tracks around the world (and, as a reminder, Ford has no looks to run in IMSA or the 24 Hours of Daytona in 2027), while its fresh “Go Like Hell” ad campaign—directed by Zac Snyder and narrated by Matt Damon—will make regular appearances on your various screens for the rest of the year. Including this one, if you click on the video below.

In a recent development, executive Editor Mike Austin has worked as a writer, editor, and occasional video host across titles such as Car and Driver, Autoblog, Popular Mechanics, and Hemmings (plus a few more). Prior to joining Road & Track he finally put his engineering degrees to use as an EV analyst. His personal cars skew slightly oddball, including a 1991 Honda Beat, 2001 Volkswagen Eurovan, 1987 Alfa Romeo Spider, and 2007 Saab 9-3 wagon.

Welcome to Car and Driver’s Testing Hub, where we zoom in on the test numbers. We’ve been pushing vehicles to their limits since 1956 to provide objective data to bolster our subjective impressions (you can see how we test here).

Sources indicate that the debut of the 2026 Lexus ES brought a full overhaul to the luxury sedan, which included a revamped hybrid variant. The new generation comes with fresh styling, a longer wheelbase, and an updated powertrain. In our testing, a 2026 ES350h was considerably quicker than a 2023 Lexus ES300h F Sport Handling, which was the last ES hybrid we tested.

See all results for latest 2026 Lexus ES for sale near 07017.

In our recent test of the ES350h, the updated sedan sprinted to 60 mph in 6.6 seconds, while the 2023 car more or less jogged its way to the 60-mph mark in 7.9 seconds. That’s a huge improvement, and one that took us by surprise, given that the fresh car doesn’t look drastically more powerful than the old one on paper. That’s to say nothing of the additional 352 pounds of weight in the new car either.

According to recent reports, so, where did all the extra quickness come from? Well, we can think of several places. For starters, the 2026 ES hybrid is more powerful, even if the numbers don’t jump off the page. The powertrain, which features a 2.5-liter four-cylinder engine, now churns out 244 horsepower, up from 215 in the 2023 ES. Along with a more powerful engine, the updated hybrid system uses a larger and more powerful electric drive motor than the previous generation. Lexus also now offers the gas-electric ES with all-wheel drive for the first time, and that’s the version we tested, with the additional traction helping offset the new car’s weight gain.

The fresh generation also moved from a 3.39:1 axle ratio to a 3.44:1 axle ratio, a change that increases low-end torque at the wheels and makes the newer car somewhat punchier off the line. Lastly, the 2026 car gets a larger hybrid battery that can provide more horsepower than the smaller unit in the previous ES.

None of the changes are individually earth-shattering—especially with the extra 352 pounds of weight—but add them together, and the ES hybrid is a much quicker car than before.

Prevost unveils Electric coach bus: 600 hp, 540 kWh, 250-mile range

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1034 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Prevost, the Quebec coach builder owned by Volvo Group, has unveiled the H3-45 Electric, its first battery-electric motorcoach.
  • The H3-45 is Prevost’s flagship and one of the most common highway coaches in North America.
  • Prevost first committed to an electric coach back in April 2022, when it announced a five-year electrification program backed by the Quebec government.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Prevost, the Quebec coach builder owned by Volvo Group, has unveiled the H3-45 Electric, its first battery-electric motorcoach. It gets a 540 kWh Volvo battery, 450 kW (600 hp) from two electric motors, and both CCS1 and MCS charging as standard.

The H3-45 is Prevost’s flagship and one of the most common highway coaches in North America. Prevost is pitching the electric version as the same coach drivers and technicians already know, with a different powertrain.

Prevost first committed to an electric coach back in April 2022, when it announced a five-year electrification program backed by the Quebec government. That plan included a 100% electric coach and a retrofit kit to convert existing diesel coaches. The coach is now here. Prevost hasn’t remarked anything fresh about the retrofit kit.

Recent findings suggest that everything that moves the coach comes from Volvo. Prevost’s product page describes a single drive unit that combines two electric motors, an 8-speed automated manual transmission, and an oil retarder, rated at 450 kW (600 hp). Prevost’s tagline for it is “more power than diesel.”.

The gearbox is the interesting part. Volvo’s own BZR Electric coach chassis in Europe uses a 2-speed automated transmission, but a 45-foot North American coach spends most of its life at highway speed and on long grades, and more gears help keep the motors in their efficient range. Prevost claims 97% motor efficiency across the working range, and drivers get adjustable regenerative braking for descents.

The battery system is made of six Volvo Cube2 units on a 600V architecture, for 540 kWh of total capacity. The brochure specifies 459 kWh of usable energy “across the full battery life,” so Prevost is holding back about 15% as a buffer.

The packs are liquid-cooled and IP6K9K-rated, and they use the same VCS2B coolant as the diesel H3-45. Volvo also backs every battery for refurbishment, second life, or recycling.

Sources indicate that prevost rates the coach at “up to 250 miles (400 km)” of range. But the footnote under that number indicates typical energy use runs up to 2.25 kWh per mile (1.40 kWh/km).

Do the math with Prevost’s own figures: 459 kWh of usable energy at 2.25 kWh/mile is about 204 miles, or roughly 328 km. Reaching 250 miles requires averaging about 1.84 kWh/mile. So 250 miles is the best case, and operators should strategy around closer to 200 miles before keeping any reserve for the return to the depot.

Also, an energy buffer of almost 80 kWh is quite massive.

Sources indicate that on a CCS1 charger at up to 350 kW, a 20-80% charge takes about 55 minutes, according to Prevost. The Megawatt Charging System (MCS) cuts that to about 35 minutes. The charge port is positioned for pull-through truck-stop stalls, and Prevost says no adapter is needed on public networks.

Those numbers also tell you how fast MCS actually charges this coach. Going from 20% to 80% of 459 kWh means adding about 275 kWh. Doing that in 35 minutes averages roughly 470 kW. That’s a lot faster than CCS1, but nowhere near a megawatt.

Recent findings suggest that the value of MCS here is access as much as speed. Megawatt chargers are being built for electric semi trucks, like the first MCS truck charge in North America at EV Realty’s San Bernardino hub, and newer dispensers like Kempower’s dual CCS and MCS charger serve both connectors. A coach that can pull into those stalls has a lot more charging options on the highway.

Industry observers note that the rest of the spec sheet reads like a regular H3-45: up to 52 passengers, Cloud One Premium seating, Prevost Driver Assist, LED headlights, five monitors, automatic tag-axle unload, and a kneeling system. 360-degree cameras and a winter package are optional.

Industry observers note that prevost markets the coach as a certified zero-emission vehicle and leans hard on grant eligibility in its brochure. There’s one catch in the fine print. The optional cold-weather heater is diesel-fired, and it produces emissions when it runs. For Canadian and northern US operators, that’s probably the option most of them will tick.

Prevost didn’t include pricing or a delivery date in its announcement. Jay Menard, who runs Prevost’s ZEV programs, told Electric Autonomy that pilots start in early 2027 and that production deliveries should begin around mid-August 2027.

Prevost isn’t first here. Its main North American rival, MCI, unveiled its J4500 CHARGE electric coach in 2021 with a 544 kWh battery and more than 200 miles of rated range. So Prevost is arriving about five years later with essentially the same battery size.

Industry observers note that what Prevost brings is a single-OEM drivetrain from Volvo, more power, a multi-speed gearbox, and MCS. It also keeps the electric version on the same platform as the diesel H3-45. And Prevost confirmed in September that its 2027 Volvo D13 diesel meets the new EPA and CARB standards. The diesel H3-45 isn’t going anywhere.

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn more ›.

You don’t have to be a hardcore prepper to put together a solid emergency kit. But, buying supplies isn’t always fun. That’s why we put together this list of Black Friday deals that can save you money along the way. We organized the picks around FEMA’s Ready.gov basic disaster supplies list, because building a kit yourself means you know how every piece works before the lights go out.

Skip what you already own. If you have a working flashlight, a roll of duct tape or a sturdy bin, put the money toward backup power, water and car gear instead. Bottled water, canned food, a manual can opener, prescriptions, small bills, pet food and copies of your ID come from the grocery store or your filing cabinet, not a deal post. If you’re starting from zero, Athena Aktipis’s guide to a starter go-bag and car kit reveals how little it takes to begin. We didn’t find Black Friday discounts on NOAA weather radios or name-brand first aid kits, so buy a hand-crank weather alert radio and a stocked first aid kit at full price rather than settling for a no-name bundle.

Cold weather is hard on car batteries, and a jump starter means you don’t need a second car or a stranger with cables to get moving. The NOCO Boost X GBX45 costs $99.96 at Amazon. NOCO rates it at 1,250 peak amps for gas engines up to 6.5 liters and diesels up to 4.0 liters, with spark-proof clamps and reverse-polarity protection. Its 60W USB-C port works in both directions, so it doubles as a power bank for a phone stuck in a stalled car, and a 100-lumen light with SOS and strobe modes is built in. Owners of big trucks with larger diesels should look at the Weego 70 in the list below instead.

Industry observers note that not everything in an outage kit should need a charging cable. The Maglite ML300L runs on four D cells, and Maglite rates it at up to 1,002 lumens, a 511-meter beam and up to 434 hours of runtime on its Eco setting. That makes it the light you leave in a drawer for years and grab when everything rechargeable is dead. It’s long and heavy, so pair it with a headlamp for hands-free work. Amazon has it for $42.29, down from $59.99, and our emergency lighting guide covers more options.

At $227 on Amazon, about half off its $449 list price, the Elite 30 V2 is the least expensive way into a real power station in this sale. Bluetti rates its 288Wh LiFePO4 battery for more than 3,000 cycles and says it recharges to 80 percent in 45 minutes, so it can refill fast when the power comes back between storms. The 600W inverter is enough for a modem and router, lamps, and phone and laptop charging. The trade-off is capacity: 288Wh won’t run a full-size refrigerator for long, so think of it as backup for electronics and lights, not the kitchen. At about 9.5 pounds, it’s light enough to move from the bedroom to the living room as the night goes on.

These keep phones alive when the power station is busy or you’re away from it, starting with the EcoFlow Rapid 20,000mAh power bank at $29.99.

The NOCO Boost X GBX45 is covered above, and the list below adds bigger jump starters plus the gear that keeps a car battery from dying in the first place.

The Maglite ML300L is covered above, and the Coast FL85R headlamp at $34.96 is the hands-free pick for clearing snow or checking a breaker panel in the dark.

Ready.gov calls for a gallon of water per person per day, and the Scepter containers below hold 2.5 gallons each; run any camp stove outdoors only, never inside, because of carbon monoxide.

Generators, camp stoves and space heaters all come out during long outages, so a battery carbon monoxide alarm like the First Alert CO400 matters as much as any light in this post.

The Bluetti Elite 30 V2 and Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 are covered above, and the stations below run from 256Wh to 2,048Wh.

Need to keep a fridge, a router and a houseful of phones going through a long outage? The Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 is $469.99 at Amazon, 41 percent off its $799 list price. Anker lists 1,024Wh of LiFePO4 capacity, 2,000W of continuous output (3,000W peak) and a 10ms UPS switchover, so gear plugged into it stays on when the grid drops. It also refills from the wall in 49 minutes at 1,600W once you turn that mode on in the Anker app. The catches are weight and cold: it’s 24.9 pounds, and Anker’s charging range starts at 32°F, so store it indoors rather than in an unheated garage. See how it compares in our guide to the best portable power stations.

If a storm or fire could force you out of the house, our guide to building a bug-out bag covers what goes inside, and these bags keep it together.

A multitool handles quick repairs, and the Rubbermaid totes keep the whole kit in one place where everyone in the house can find it.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that suzuki left the U.S.
  • The Ignis is Suzuki’s first subcompact electric car developed for global markets, but its roots are in Japan.
  • A 26-kilowatt-hour lithium iron phosphate battery sits under the floor of Suzuki’s dedicated Heartect-e electric platform.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that suzuki left the U.S. car market in 2012, but it still builds the kind of small hatchbacks European buyers have long favored, now also powered by electricity. Its latest is the Ignis EV, a city car that measures just 11 feet 9 inches long (3.57 meters). It’s due in Europe in summer 2027, when it will face a new generation of small EVs from both European and Chinese automakers.

The Ignis is Suzuki’s first subcompact electric car developed for global markets, but its roots are in Japan. The manufacturer recently launched the e Sky there, an electric kei car that supplies the basis for the Ignis’s body and powertrain. The Ignis still has the typical kei proportions (it's tall and narrow), but Suzuki claims it took the car onto European city streets and winding roads to tune the suspension and power delivery, making it more appealing to the people it hopes will buy one.

A 26-kilowatt-hour lithium iron phosphate battery sits under the floor of Suzuki’s dedicated Heartect-e electric platform. Yes, that really is what it's called. Up front, the motor, inverter, and reduction gears share a single compact assembly that sends 90 horsepower and 98 pound-feet (133 Nm) to the front wheels. Suzuki indicates it chose LFP for safety and longevity, but it hasn’t given the European car a range or charging figure yet.

The Ignis EV has a very tight 29.5-foot (9-meter) turning circle. Its overhangs are tiny, giving it a wheel-at-each-corner stance that looks unique while maximizing available interior room. The LED signatures at both ends take their shape from digital numerals, and the dark pillars give the roof a floating look.

Inside, a curve runs from the dashboard into the doors, with a wide display and a ceramic-inspired storage tray across the dash. Suzuki President Toshihiro Suzuki credits the company’s decades of building Japanese mini vehicles for its ability to provide a genuinely usable cabin in such a small footprint.

For decades, European brands had most of this business to themselves. If you wanted an inexpensive car that could squeeze down a narrow street, Fiat would happily sell you a Panda, Renault a Twingo and Volkswagen an Up. Chinese automakers see an opening as those buyers go electric.

Leapmotor brought the T03 to Europe through its partnership with Stellantis, while BYD adapted its Chinese-market Seagull for Europe and called it the Dolphin Surf. Driving the latter, what stood out to me was how well it drove, how little felt cheap, and how much kit it had for its sub-€20,000 starting price.

It has been revealed that by the time the Ignis arrives next year, European buyers will have had plenty of practice shopping for small EVs. Renault has revived both the 5 and the Twingo as electric cars, and there’s also the related Dacia Spring. Volkswagen has the ID. Polo, Cupra has the Raval, and Skoda has the Epiq, and there definitely seems to be demand for them. In September, a major VW dealer group reported more than 30,000 orders for the ID. Polo and a waiting list stretching to ten months.

That leaves one substantial question for the little Suzuki. What will it cost? Consider the redesigned Dacia Spring. Dacia moved production from China to Slovenia, shared the electric Twingo’s underpinnings, and produced a car that starts at €17,900 in Italy. It gets up to 155 miles (250 kilometers) of WLTP range from a battery only slightly larger than the one in the Ignis.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

EA Sports has revealed 3 new Heroes coming to FC 26 Ultimate Team as part of Team 1 of the Winter Wildcards promo: Ivan Zamorano, Claudio Pizarro and Jill Scott.

The Bayern and Werder Bremen legend Claudio Pizarro is famously the Bundesliga’s oldest ever player, after turning out well past 40 years of age - up front no less. But he’s making an appearance in FC 26 because he won the Hero Vote Poll a few months ago, with the Peruvian edging out notable nutter Steffan Effenberg and the prolific Brazilian striker, Elber.

The love for South American Heroes continues with Ivan Zamorano presented in his Real Madrid guise rather than part of the unbelievably stacked Inter squad which featured legends and Icons ranging from current Atletico Madrid manager Diego Simeone to Javier Zanetti and Ronaldo Nazario.

And probably most interestingly, Queen of the Jungle and centurion Lioness, Jill Scott, is also coming to shore up the midfield with a card which fits the “Gullit Gang” pre-requisite of all face stats over 80 - including a dominant 91 physical befitting her role as one of the most recognisable enforcers in women’s football.

Whether her in-game body type will actually let her put that strength out on the pitch (she will surely also have Bruiser) remains to be seen, but she could easily have the gangly aura of Patrick Vieira if the rest of her PlayStyles are right.

New Ultimate Team Heroes have been added mid-season before, including the likes of Enzo Francescoli in FC 24, but 3 at once looks to indicate that EA is leaning on Heroes to add fan-favourite players to the game with a lower threshold than Icons.

Plus they can be given away for free without upsetting the power curve as much as Icons, as shown by the free Classic XI Heroes handed out recently (I got Mario Gomez, F).

The rest of the Winter Wildcards team features a host of equally famous, and now infamous, players with some featuring 99 stats and alternative positions.

Highlights include striker and CAM versions of Balon D’or holder Ousmane Dembele, but also everyone’s love-to-hate Low Driven Shot master, Claudia Pina.

There are also incredibly strong-looking Gabriel and Fede Valverde cards, as well as downgraded, and therefore hopefully cheaper, versions of Icons like Johan Cruyff.

Tested: The 2028 Volvo XC60 T8 Is the Rangiest Plug-In Hybrid

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1160 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Roadandtrack

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that on the journey to the future of automotive propulsion, Volvo was an early adopter of the all-electric ethos.
  • Industry observers note that our expert editors test every vehicle we review.
  • Recent findings suggest that we have always appreciated the charms of the current-generation XC60, with a substantial package of changes sharpening its case for a few more years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that on the journey to the future of automotive propulsion, Volvo was an early adopter of the all-electric ethos. The Swedish automaker initially vowed to stop selling all gasoline-powered cars—including hybrids—by 2030. A few years and three fresh all-electric models later, Volvo has radically altered that initiative and will continue to sell hybrid models past that point. That includes extending the life of the existing lineup, with the already-near-decade-old second-gen XC60 getting a new T8 powertrain, which gives it the longest pure electric range of any plug-in hybrid on sale in the U.S.

Industry observers note that our expert editors test every vehicle we review. Read more about how we test and review cars here.

Recent findings suggest that we have always appreciated the charms of the current-generation XC60, with a substantial package of changes sharpening its case for a few more years. Visually, the most obvious changes are a newly introduced front end incorporating LED matrix headlights and smaller revisions at the rear. The technical highlight is an improved 78-mile EPA electric range from a mammoth 37.9-kWh battery pack, this delivered to a motor on the rear axle; a smaller starter-generator can add modest assistance at the front as well. Volvo quotes a peak electric output of 208 hp, with the 2.0-liter turbo four that drives the front wheels able to deliver 247 horses. Inside, the XC60 receives small material and trim adjustments.

Engine: 1969-cc turbocharged inline-four, hybridized.

Power: 455 hp (peak system output).

Torque: 494 lb-ft (peak system output).

Transmission: eight-speed automatic, all-wheel drive.

As I pulled into Copenhagen’s morning traffic, Volvo’s Pure drive mode, which idles the gasoline-powered engine in favor of an all-electric experience, felt prudent among the multitude of commuting bicyclists. Silent running was entirely suited to the Scandinavian environment, but the XC60 T8 wasn’t stumbling over itself either when running under electrical power, Volvo having significantly juiced up the electric motor alongside the bigger battery pack.

Recent findings suggest that while 208 hp in Pure EV mode has to work against 4855 pounds of weight, the T8 felt well suited to both metropolitan driving and the open road, the effective surge of electrical power proving itself on highways and the 9.9-mile-long Øresund Link that connects Denmark to Malmö, Sweden. Power delivery definitely wasn’t as aggressive as that of a spicy EV, but it wasn’t gentle either, and the electric motor had enough punch to drive the XC60 without me yearning for the gas engine to intervene. Something that won’t happen unless the accelerator is pushed to a kickdown position or by switching drive modes. The 78-mile EPA range is genuinely class-leading, and selecting the T8’s Charge mode rapidly replenished e-miles when selected.

Industry observers note that switching from the Pure to Hybrid mode was where the real fun began. And fun isn’t too strong a word for the unlikely performance of the split hybrid system as the 2.0-liter turbo adds its contribution to the front axle, giving a combined peak of 455 hp and what Volvo claims is 4.5-second 0–60-mph capability. In practice, the XC60 T8 felt shockingly quick, rapidly spinning up the speedometer at wide-open throttle. The accelerator has a two-part action, with softer response at the top of its travel metering electrical power before the combustion horses arrive with a suddenness. This was fun, but the transition also felt a bit too obvious considering how subtle some hybrids now are. Switching it up to Power mode refocused the powertrain by keeping the engine running and solved the on-and-off drama. The eight-speed automatic transmission shifts without drama, and there’s enough electrical torque that I didn’t even want for the missing steering-wheel paddle shifters.

Sources indicate that we liked the way the pre-facelift XC60 T8 drove, and the upcoming version impressed as much. Volvos are traditionally heavy and somewhat leisurely to respond, but the XC60 successfully belied its scale with impressively neutral handling on narrow Swedish country roads. My XC60 test vehicle was fitted with the optional air suspension and active shock absorbers, fighting body roll and delivering a reactive front end.

It has been revealed that similarly, Volvo’s power-steering system was smooth and direct, though both weight settings skewed overly light for my tastes. It’s not as overtly sporty as some performance SUVs, but its combination of qualities was definitely appealing. My only complaints were a somewhat agricultural soundtrack under full throttle and what was often a harsh ride over rough surfaces, bumps, and imperfections being transferred into the cabin.

Sources indicate that I didn’t get a chance to plug in the XC60, but Volvo remarked the 2028 model can charge at speeds up to 7.2 kWh. All told, the XC60 PHEV will take around 5.7 hours to fully charge up at maximum speed.

Sources indicate that volvo has long succeeded at creating minimalist cabins without them looking sparse or cheap, and the XC60 continues to carry that torch with a few exceptions. And one of these exceptions was the 11.2-inch center touchscreen, which has been blown out of the casing found on previous model years to take over the entire console.

Annoyingly, climate-control functions are integrated into this display with multiple menus required for adjustment, the Android Auto software beneath it starting to show its age. Similarly, Apple CarPlay is only available through a wired connection—that’s so 2017. That noted, the infotainment system was easy to operate despite its limitations. Plus, Volvo has perfected the art of displaying turn-by-turn directions on the instrument cluster; a dial speedometer and tachometer sit opposite each other with an appropriately scaled navigation map centered in between.

Beyond the technology, the XC60’s interior was a charming place to spend time. Latest Scandinavian-inspired materials on the dashboard included brushed wood and knit fabric, which looked upmarket and were pleasing to the touch. The light leather seats were firm yet comfortable and included massage, heating, and cooling functions, which can be operated all at once. Other notable interior design wins include a wooden sliding cup-holder cover, an alluring crystal shift knob, and satisfying brushed steel door handles. The Bowers & Wilkins stereo system on my test car was fantastic, and Volvo deserves points for retaining a traditional volume knob, as well as tactile buttons to skip songs.

It has been revealed that if you want a properly long-range plug-in hybrid SUV, the Volvo XC60 may be your best option, at least for now. The next longest-range mid-size luxury SUV option is the Mercedes-Benz GLC Hybrid, which offers 54 all-electric miles. Toyota also offers a RAV4 Plug-In Hybrid with 52 miles of range. Volvo has not declared finalized U.S. pricing for the 2028 XC60 T8 yet.

Sources indicate that volvo interiors are well known for minimalist luxury, but even the Swedes can’t help themselves from including an easter egg here and there. Placed on the right edge of the passenger-side dashboard, Volvo has engraved a miniature Swedish flag on the brushed aluminum trim.

  • The Whale is the first flagship multi-purpose vehicle (MPV) from BYD’s Ocean series.
  • BYD unveiled the Whale for the first time at the Guangzhou Auto Show on November 27, with a launch set for the first quarter of 2027.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that BYD’s new flagship MPV is not your average minivan. The Whale can drive over 559 miles (900 km) on a single charge, charge in as little as five minutes, and it’s packed with BYD’s latest tech.

The Whale is the first flagship multi-purpose vehicle (MPV) from BYD’s Ocean series. BYD has several sub-brands, including Denza, Yangwang, and Fang Cheng Bao, and sells vehicles under two primary lineups: Ocean and Dynasty.

BYD unveiled the Whale for the first time at the Guangzhou Auto Show on November 27, with a launch set for the first quarter of 2027.

Measuring 5,270 mm long, 1,996 mm wide, and 1,815 mm tall, with a 3,130 mm wheelbase, BYD’s newest minivan is slightly longer than the Chrysler Pacifica.

The Whale will be available in both plug-in hybrid (PHEV) and pure electric (EV) powertrains. Both will use BYD’s latest Blade Batteries 2.0. The PHEV version will offer a pure-electric CLTC range of 248 miles (400 km), while the EV variant offers over 559 miles (900 km) of range on a single charge.

With BYD’s Flash Charging tech, the electric minivan can charge from 10% to 70% in just five minutes.

For a full recharge, or to go from 10% to 97%, it takes only nine minutes. Even in temperatures as low as -30°C(-22°F), it takes just 3 minutes longer, or 12 minutes total.

Leading up to its debut, camouflaged prototypes were spotted with a boxy design that looked closer to a traditional gas-powered MPV.

However, the Whale looks better than expected. It adopts BYD’s updated Ocean design with smooth edges and a double-layer staggered grille.

BYD didn’t reveal many details outside of confirming the name and showcasing the design. With LiDAR on the roof, the Whale will offer BYD’s latest Advanced Driver Assistance System (ADAS).

The Whale will go on sale in the first quarter of 2027, joining the Dynasty Series Xia, Linghui M9, and Denza D9 as BYD’s fourth MPV.

Prices will be revealed closer to launch, but the Whale is expected to start at around 300,000 yuan ($45,000), filling the gap between the Xia, which starts at 249,800 yuan ($37,500), and the Denza D9 at 359,800 yuan ($54,000).

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ionna, the EV charging network that ranked first in J.D.
  • The company, which usually charges an average of $0.40/kilowatt-hour, is now asking for $0.20/kWh plus tax at all its DC fast charging stations in the United States.
  • For long-distance travel, the slashed charging rates can make a significant difference.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ionna, the EV charging network that ranked first in J.D. Power’s latest public charging satisfaction survey, has slashed prices at its stations across the country for Thanksgiving weekend.

The company, which usually charges an average of $0.40/kilowatt-hour, is now asking for $0.20/kWh plus tax at all its DC fast charging stations in the United States. That’s a 50% discount, and drivers don’t have to do anything special to get it—just plug in and pay, either through the automaker’s official smartphone app, the on-site payment terminals, or the Presto app for Tesla owners who want to enjoy the Autocharge function.

For long-distance travel, the slashed charging rates can make a significant difference. A single 50-kilowatt-hour session that used to cost $20 will now be just $10 plus tax, but seeing how many people are traveling across the country these days, multiple sessions will be necessary, driving the cost savings even further.

Industry observers note that and it’s not like the cost reduction comes with any strings attached. Ionna uses 400-kilowatt chargers from Alpitronic exclusively, so there’s plenty of wiggle room for even the most power-hungry EVs out there. What’s more, many stalls have dual cords for each port, with a CCS connector and a NACS connector, so charging adapters aren’t needed at most locations.

Separately, Ionna has discounts for several automakers, including Mercedes-Benz, BMW, General Motors, and Stellantis.

The charging operator installed its first stalls in 2024, and it has wasted no time expanding its footprint promptly. On its second anniversary, Ionna celebrated by opening its 100th site, and the company now has 229 sites and nearly 1,900 ports nationwide, according to the Department of Energy's Alternative Fuels Data Center (AFDC). Still, the charging network is not slowing down, with dozens of locations under construction and prepares to introduce 500-kW chargers in the near future.

Industry observers note that most EV brands support Plug & Charge at Ionna, with Tesla recently getting Autocharge functionality through a third-party smartphone application. Ionna itself doesn’t have a smartphone app, instead relying on automakers and third-party apps to integrate its locations. So far, this approach has turned out to be quite successful, with J.D. Power’s latest public charging survey putting the operator first, ahead of Tesla and the rest of the competition.

TVR Returns From The Dead. Again

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, would you wait a decade for a new car?
  • Industry observers note that delays were reportedly caused by the failure to secure funding to build a factory in Wales among other crises.
  • There isn’t room for any detailed history of TVR here, but the original incarnation of the sport car maker collapsed into bankruptcy in 2006, having become both famous and infamous for brutish, fiber-bodied models including the 1990 Griffith, 1996 Cerbera and 1999 Tuscan Speed Six.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, would you wait a decade for a new car? That’s the situation for anybody who raised their hand to buy the TVR Griffith when it was announced as far back as 2017. R&T’s own interest in the story faded soon after the reborn British brand announced the car was going to be heavily delayed. But, in truth, nobody realized how long the wait would be.

Industry observers note that delays were reportedly caused by the failure to secure funding to build a factory in Wales among other crises. It’s fair to say that the interest of most onlookers, and surely all of the potential buyers , faded as the excuses piled up. But after a change in ownership last year, TVR's new parent MOTV Group has declared that the Griffith will be produced at the Lotus factory in Hethel, with the first customer deliveries “planned for 2028,” although those likely restricted to buyers in the U.K.

There isn’t room for any detailed history of TVR here, but the original incarnation of the sport car maker collapsed into bankruptcy in 2006, having become both famous and infamous for brutish, fiber-bodied models including the 1990 Griffith, 1996 Cerbera and 1999 Tuscan Speed Six. Also the semi-mythical, one-of-one Speed 12 which was a star of early Gran Turismo games. TVR was reborn in 2013 after software entrepreneur Les Edgar bought the rights to the brand; according to public records in the U.K., Edgar resigned from the firm board earlier this month.

MOTV Group was previously known as Charge Holdings, with subsidiary Charge Cars planning to build an electrified restomod version of the 1967 Ford Mustang before it, too, collapsed into bankruptcy. In 2025, Charge was saved by a group of investors and subsequently merged with TVR.

Recent findings suggest that the official announcement of TVR’s latest return was accompanied by an image of what appears to be the 2017 concept car, now wrapped in a new disguise. Comparison of the images reveals the same headlight position, panel lines, side-exit exhaust and identically patterned wheels. MOTV indicates the car will have a spaceframe chassis, a composite body, a V-8 engine with a manual transmission, and rear-wheel drive - all details aligning the 2017 version.

The original proposal was for the new Griffith to use the iStream production process created by Gordon Murray’s then technology company, but this subsidiary has since been sold to ForSeven, which subsequently acquired McLaren Automotive which presumably owns the rights. So It will be interesting to discover if this technology-sharing partnership remains in place. Similarly, there is no confirmation that Cosworth is still involved in fettling the Ford Coyote V-8 that was meant to power the car as was originally unveiled.

Beyond the above facts the official announcement was short on details beyond naming the senior executive team, these including CEO Paul Abercrombie and CTO Steve MacManus, who was formerly an engineering vice president at Tesla and who seems to have worked on the aborted Apple car project.

Can TVR manage it this time? Given the soap opera of the brand’s recent history, there remains a substantial question mark over that one. As does the more relevant unknown for most R&T readers as to whether there is any chance a reborn Griffith would ever reach the U.S. It would be fun if it did, but let’s not get our hopes up yet.

In a recent development, after starting in radio, Mike Duff broke into writing about cars more than 25 years ago. Since then, he has reviewed several thousand cars, working for major outlets on both sides of the Atlantic. In the U.K. he held senior staff positions with CAR, Autocar and evo, and in the U.S. he wrote for MPH and Autoweek before becoming Car and Driver’s European Editor for ten years. Being a Brit means he also understands most of the rules of cricket.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that heartopia developer XD Games has delivered the news anyone who tried out the life sim game had been waiting for. The Animal Crossing-like cozy multiplayer game will finally arrive on January 7 across Android, iOS, and PC - with one caveat.

The Steam version won’t actually launch on that date, and will instead go live at some other point in the future. You will be able to play it on PC through TapTap, which is the same emulator you may be familiar with from beta.

Pre-registration is open on the official website for all platforms. If you throw in your email address, you’ll receive a bundle of in-game items at launch. You’ll get 4,000 Gold, 20 Wishing Stars, 400 Moonlight Crystal, and 60 Exhibition Passes.

Interestingly, XD Games isn’t saying what you can expect from the launch build - in terms of content - just yet. Those details will be revealed closer to the January launch, so perhaps expect them in the first few days of the year.

It has been revealed that if you created a character in either (or both) of the recent closed beta tests, you’ll also receive the Blueberry Crossbody Bag in-game cosmetic. If you made it to level 18 in either test, you’ll also get the Star Mascot Head cosmetic. Both items will be available to claim at launch.

It has been revealed that we’ve spent a lot of time playing the game’s recent tests, and we’ve put together some early guides on how to get Roaming Oak Timber, how to unlock and upgrade hobbies and more. We also have a few cooking recipes to share with you.

Volvo Is Bringing Humanoid Robots Into Its Factories. Here's When They'll Start Working

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Volvo, the maker of the EX60 electric crossover, wants to replace some factory workers with humanoid robots that are capable of doing repetitive tasks without complaining about back pain.
  • To make that happen, the car manufacturer has brought in the first Aeon units at its factory in Ghent, Belgium, where humans are presently training them to do various tasks.
  • Volvo Cars is training AEON humanoid robots for future work in factories.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Volvo, the maker of the EX60 electric crossover, wants to replace some factory workers with humanoid robots that are capable of doing repetitive tasks without complaining about back pain.

To make that happen, the car manufacturer has brought in the first Aeon units at its factory in Ghent, Belgium, where humans are presently training them to do various tasks. Volvo noted that it aims to support employees in repetitive and “ergonomically challenging work,” and it’s not the only car manufacturer that’s leaning towards replacing humans with robots.

Volvo Cars is training AEON humanoid robots for future work in factories.

While fixed robotic arms have been a staple of automotive factories for decades, some brands are now investing a lot of time and money in artificial intelligence-powered robots that can do tasks where components don’t always land in the same exact spot. So-called pick-and-place jobs are gradually being taken over by robots, with Tesla, General Motors, Ford, and Rivian slowly but surely filling their factories with complex robots.

Volvo is no different, and while the first humanoids shipped to the manufacturer’s plant in Ghent are only being trained right now, they’ll gradually start going to work in real conditions starting in mid 2027, the Swedish manufacturer stated.

Right now, Volvo Cars is using imitation learning to teach the robot how to pick up and place certain components into two fixtures with high precision. Through the learning process, the team will gradually make the work more challenging, adding multiple parts, moving around the production area, and interacting with the plant’s automated systems.

“Aeon’s humanoid design means it can fit into our production as it is today, alongside our teams and existing automation,” says Magnus Nilsson, Chief Manufacturing Officer at Volvo Cars. “Our aim is for humanoid robots to take on some of the most physically demanding tasks and help make work more ergonomic for our people.”.

The robot chosen by Volvo looks like a human, but it doesn’t have feet. Instead, the 5.4-foot (1.65-meter) robot moves on wheels and is capable of reaching up to 5.3 miles per hour (8.6 kilometers per hour). It weighs 132 pounds (60 kilograms) and can carry up to 22 lbs (10 kg). Several cameras and sensors are used to capture its surroundings and handle parts with precision.

#155451. Industry News: Tested: 1979 Buick Century Turbo Coupe Is a Rolling Contradiction

Industry News: Tested: 1979 Buick Century Turbo Coupe Is a Rolling Contradiction

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2343 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Caranddriver

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A paradox, according to a well­-thumbed copy of Webster’s New World, is a statement that seems contradictory, but may be true.
  • On the other hand we have this Tur­bo Coupe posturing about in its rackish, spoilered finery, squatting on its we­-mean-business fat tires, its twin pipes burbling, acting more Trans Am than Buick.
  • It has been revealed that buick started making out-of-character performance noises a few years ago when its chief engineer, Lloyd Reuss, and a band of enthusiastic young engi­neers decided to crank up a turbocharg­ing project for the V-6 engine.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

From the June 1979 issue of Car and Driver.

A paradox, according to a well­-thumbed copy of Webster’s New World, is a statement that seems contradictory, but may be true. Which brings us imme­diately to the Buick Century Turbo Coupe. On one hand it most definitely is a Buick, which is automatically a state­ment. As most of us were growing up, the Buicks in our lives belonged to the family doctor or other such community pillars. Buicks were sedate, relatively ex­pensive cars—stop-offs on the way up the GM ladder for the man with the growing bank account, or the highest reasonable aspirations for the workaday man who longed to rise out of Ford and Chevy land.

On the other hand we have this Tur­bo Coupe posturing about in its rackish, spoilered finery, squatting on its we­-mean-business fat tires, its twin pipes burbling, acting more Trans Am than Buick. A contradiction.

It has been revealed that buick started making out-of-character performance noises a few years ago when its chief engineer, Lloyd Reuss, and a band of enthusiastic young engi­neers decided to crank up a turbocharg­ing project for the V-6 engine. Their ef­forts were first seen in the 1975 Indy pace car, which also sported some very un-Buick-like suspension. In 1977 Buick offered a slick Sport Coupe variation on the LeSabre and Regal theme. The Le­Sabre version we tested was so good it elicited comments like “a breath of fresh air for people who’ve hungered to own a good-handling American car.” And one exuberant staffer stated all it needed was a three-pointed star on the hood to make it a Mercedes-class piece. In 1978 the turbo motor went into pro­duction, and the stage was set for this year's Turbo Coupe.

See all results for used cars for sale near 48429.

According to recent reports, bruce Robinson is a project engineer at Buick’s Flint, Michigan, headquar­ters, and one of those enthusiastic types Reuss brought in to spice up Buick’s slide-rule department. Reuss is gone now—he’s chief engineer over at Chev­rolet—but Robinson and the Reuss en­thusiasm still exist. Robinson was as­signed the Turbo Coupe. He didn’t build it single-handedly, but as much as any car that pops off the line can be stated to be one man’s baby, the Turbo Coupe is his.

“We wanted to go from GT, like the LeSabre and Regal Sport Coupes, to All Out,” Robinson explains. “We wanted to make it go, and handle, and stop like no other Buick.”.

In a recent development, he did it, he explains, by creating what Buick now calls the FE1 package, a giant step up from the existing FE2, which is Buick’s equivalent of Chevro­let’s famous F41 handling upgrade. The FE1, available only on the Turbo Coupe, is basically stiffer springs, steer­ing changes, and wider wheels. The front spring rates have been increased from the regular Sport Coupe specs of 365 pounds per inch to a giganto 440. Rear springs are up to 140 lbs/in from 125. (For further comparison, the base V-6 Century coupe has spring rates, front/rear, of 300/115.) Anti-roll bars are the same for FE1 and FE2: 32 mm front, 22 mm rear; but another substantial up­grade for the Turbo came in the rear upper-control-arm bushings, little de­vices we don’t think much about but which have a lot to do with transient re­sponse. The base and Sport Coupe ver­sions have bushings rated at 20,000 lbs/in; the Turbo Coupe is fitted with 35,000-lbs/in bushings. Rounding out the FE2 package is a quicker steering ra­tio, 14:1 instead of 15.13:1, and P205/70R-14 radials on seven-inch rims.

See all results for used cars for sale near 48429.

But as much as we wanted to know all that good spring and tire stuff, we were even more curious about the exhaust system. It is, in a word, loud. We spent a lot of time playing with the throttle and letting off in low and second just to hear that sound-from-the-past, that Golden Oldie exhaust noise. How'd Robinson do it?

Sources indicate that the sound, he reveals, was a specifi­cally planned part of the overall image. They got it by the simple expedient of routing the exhaust into a single con­verter and then out into a pair of ex­haust pipes that carry a resonator each. No mufflers.

“A delightful byproduct,” Robinson gleefully reveals, “was an extra ten horsepower due to the reduced back pressure.” The odds on finding ten horsepower these days without spend­ing ’leventeen trillion dollars in devel­opment are about the same as Bianca and her pals dropping by your place for dinner tonight: slim to none.

That throaty exhaust note, by the way, is more evident inside the Turbo Coupe than outside. The body acts as a sound chamber to increase the effect. “The noise level passed the EPA tests,” Robinson notes, “but we’re not about to ask them to check it again to make sure.” Right.

In a recent development, so Robinson and his associates have built a Buick with all the right suspen­sion bits and pieces, they’ve come up with a creditable 175 horses to move it around, they’ve given it an exhaust sys­tem to warm the cockles of an old hot rodder’s heart, and they’ve dressed it up with spoilers and flat-black paint. Why, we had to wonder, after doing all that, did they leave out some traditional, mandatory even, performance-car parts, like a manual transmission and an in­strument panel with some gauges?

“Simple,” Robinson notes. “Money.”.

According to recent reports, adding a manual transmission would have required a complete 50,000-mile EPA durability test, and that costs hun­dreds of thousands. Ditto a different in­strument panel. Buick didn’t have any­thing on the shelf that would have bolt­ed in. Designing a new panel and tool­ing up to produce it would also have cost hundreds of thousands.

“Anything you spend on building a new model, or a new version of an exist­ing car,” Robinson explains, “you have to figure you can recover in sales.” And Buick doesn’t figure to sell too many Turbo Coupes, it turns out. It's an image car, a showroom-traffic build­er, so if you see one on the floor of your local Buick dealer, you’re probably looking at his allotment for the year. Should you jump at it?

The Turbo Coupe is easily the best-­looking of all the “aero” designs, which Buick and Olds offer in two- and four­-door versions. The improvement in looks seems to come from the simple addition of the rear-deck spoiler, which also happens to reduce overall drag, Buick reports, by a healthy 18 percent. (The two-door aero design, by the way, will be around at least through 1980; the ugly four-door is going away.).

Inside, as we’ve hinted, there is little to distinguish the Turbo Coupe from its lesser brethren. The handsome, but un­informative, instrument panel contains a tricolor turbo-boost indicator that reads out in one, A Little, and Whoosh. Our test car had vinyl buckets, and while they provide pretty good sup­port in all the right places, they are as slick as greased owl potty. Cloth is avail­able, however, and we recommend it.

Over the road, the Turbo’s yes-I-am, no-I’m-not nature surfaces again. De­spite all the good things Robinson and his merry band have wrought, the car’s manners are still rather Buick-like. Which isn’t necessarily all bad. Your teeth aren’t jarred by every tar strip, and the car is very quiet at cruise. But there is an unexpected numbness in the steering that should have been factored out. Response is good, but that all-vital feel is missing.

Despite the suspension modifications, the Turbo Coupe is still an understeer­er. That’s to be expected, so no points lost there. General Motors is a firm be­liever that understeer is safer than over­steer. Better, the reasoning goes, the in­competents plow off the road nose-first, scrubbing speed all the way, than have the tail leading the procession at prodi­gious speed. Fair enough, because the knowledgeable Trans Am or Z28 driver can put the boot into his mount at the proper time and induce some very pleasant oversteer. Not so with the Tur­bo Coupe; the little engine-that-would­-be-a-V-8 just doesn’t produce enough torque promptly enough to let you play the tail-out game with much success. The boost gauge may be up there in Whoosh, but the tail will be dutifully following the furrow the front end is plowing. We’re talking about out there at the cop-baiting, wife-scaring, dog­-cowering limit, of course. In normal brisk motoring, the suspension does a good job. There’s no willow-wallow here, thank you.

Recent findings suggest that the Coupe also does other good things. You’ll note that our comparison graphs show it at the top in acceleration ­and braking. Straight-line numbers will not disappoint.

Sources indicate that the Turbo Coupe certainly has the flash and dash Buick wants for its show­rooms, and it’s sure to draw its share of peekers and pokers and hood lifters. The traditional Buick buyer will peek and poke and then head off to the Elec­tra or LeSabre four-doors. The curious that stopped off on their way to price Trans Am and Z28s will poke and peek with a good bit more interest. And when they learn they can have a bare-bones Turbo Coupe for a little more than $6000, they may even give it some seri­ous thought. But our best guess is they’ll eventually find their way back to those other showrooms. The Turbo Coupe, as good a Buick as it is, doesn’t seem to be right for either group.

In a recent development, what we want is Bruce Robinson and his boys to turn their attention to a new Skylark Sport Coupe. Turbo that little honey, slap the FE1 package on it, and stand back. When we suggested that to Robinson, his eyes lit up with what could only be engineer-type lust. So maybe it’ll happen. And maybe it’ll even have a tachometer.

I must admit, the first night I drove the Turbo Coupe I kept putting my foot into it and running up through the gears, then backing off and doing it again and again, all the way home. The pumped-up little six, all snarling and willing, was just too inviting for me to ignore. Sometimes I’d even drop it into low and back off just to listen to the popping of the exhaust as it simmered down. I acted as silly as a newly licensed adolescent that night, but you just can’t resist playing in the Turbo Coupe. It’s that kind of car.

It has been revealed that but what turned me on the most was the message hidden within its sophisticat­ed mechanicals: a latest generation of mus­cle cars, one that pays its respects to both ecology and our tight petroleum supply, is not only possible, it’s just around the corner. All Buick has to do is work its tur­bocharging wizardry on the half-ton-­lighter Skylark front-driver and we’ll have the first of that new breed. Let us pray. —Rich Ceppos.

Sources indicate that I happen to be a firm believer in turbo­charging and all the wonderful things it can do for our cars—David E. Davis, Jr., to the contrary—but this Turbo Coupe from Buick stretches the very heartstrings of my enthusiasm. Past the limit. It’s a horrible fate for any engine as spunky as Buick’s turbo V-6. This motor should be zapping around a 2000-pound sports car or burning the tires off Buick’s chic little Skyhawk. Instead, it’s sentenced to the homeliest hunchback sedan Buick has stamped out in recent history. Grown men wince at the sight of this TR7 garage on wheels. And I wince at the thought of such an eager engine straining its heart out against a 3500-pound curb weight and an automatic transmission, without so much as a tachometer or a boost gauge to register the effort. To finish off the in­sult, this Century’s all gussied up in what I assume is Buick’s idea of a performance disguise. It looks like something the local sheriff would use to sneak up on the kids down at Shakey's. They wouldn’t be con­vinced, and neither am I. —Don Sherman.

Sources indicate that normally, when you dip the accelerator on a six-cylinder American car, it gives you the feeling you’re saving gas. Saving gas is a noble pastime but the feeling of saving gas is drudgery, right up there with Cometing out the sink.

In a recent development, that is why I think this Buick stands to give the American six-cylinder a good name. When you dip the pedal, things hap­pen. First off, the whole dashboard glows orange. (Knepper said the illumination comes from the boost light, but it’s hidden behind so many spokes and switches that I never actually saw it.) Then the exhaust turns mean and the bucket seat gets all pushy. Instead of saving gas, you get the feeling you’re hurrying.

Really, except for a count of the spark-­plug wires, there’s nothing six-cylinder about this car. It feels more like a high schooler’s hot rod, glass packs and all, and I had the urge to head on down to the drive-in and burn some rubber. I haven’t been in that mood for years. —Patrick Bedard.

Legendary game creator Vince Zampella has passed away

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that vince Zampella, known for co-creating the Call of Duty series, among many other roles, has died.
  • According to NBC, Zampella’s Ferrari hit a concrete barrier after leaving a tunnel in the San Gabriel Mountains, north of Los Angeles.
  • Vince Zampella is one of the industry’s most prolific creators.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that vince Zampella, known for co-creating the Call of Duty series, among many other roles, has died. Zampella, 55, died in a car crash in Los Angeles on Sunday. The fatal crash killed him, along with the occupant of his car.

According to NBC, Zampella’s Ferrari hit a concrete barrier after leaving a tunnel in the San Gabriel Mountains, north of Los Angeles. Zampella was unfortunately trapped in an ensuing car fire, and the passenger was ejected.

Vince Zampella is one of the industry’s most prolific creators. His storied career is long, and is responsible for some of the biggest shooter franchises in history. It started with Medal of Honor in the 90s, a game that changed WW2 shooters forever.

Zampella later co-founded the legendary Infinity Ward in 2002, the team that would go on to redefine multiplayer shooters forever. Infinity Ward is the studio responsible for the Call of Duty series, which remains one of the biggest games for publisher Activision, and the entire industry.

In a recent development, zampella then left the studio he founded in 2010 following a major fallout with Activision. He, along with longtime collaborator, Jason West, went to rival publisher EA to form Respawn Entertainment.

Industry observers note that respawn went on to create the Titanfall series, and later Apex Legends. The studio is responsible for non-shooters, of course, like the third-person action game series Star Wars Jedi. Zampella was instrumental in making the game possible, having hired God of War 3 director Stig Asmussen to helm a team within Respawn out of a desire to diversify the studio’s output and prove he can do more than make shooters.

Industry observers note that zampella had only recently met with journalists and peers at The Game Awards, where Battlefield 6 was nominated for multiple awards. Battlefield 6 is the most successful game in series history, in part as a result of Zampella’s leadership. The legendary leader was given the reigns of the struggling multiplayer shooter franchise in 2021, with a goal of finding a viable future.

Zampella’s sudden death has shaken the industry, and many mourn his loss as the news started spreading.

“We are heartbroken by the loss of Vince Zampella, a creative leader whose work shaped generations of players and helped define what modern shooters and action games could be,” EA said in a statement.

Industry observers note that “While his impact reached far beyond any one game or studio, we will remember Vince for how he showed up every day, trusting his teams, encouraging bold ideas, and believing in Battlefield and the people building it. We are deeply grateful for his leadership, his generosity, and the care he brought to everything he touched, and we will carry that forward with us.”.

  • “It’s going to run back and forth, back and forth, just like a ferry,” explains Oivind Berge, co-owner of Berge Rederi Future, in a TradeWinds interview.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Moving millions of tons of coal, sugar, and other bulk cargo is serious business, and decarbonizing that business presents a number of unique problems – but if the new BRF Froan bulk carrier proves anything, it’s that battery size isn’t one of them. The new electric cargo ship is packing an impossibly huge, 23,500 kWh battery.

Fitted with the equivalent of nearly 300 long-range electric car batteries, 130 meter (426 ft.) BRF Froam built by SOHO Marine Heavy Industry for Norwegian shipping firm Berge Rederi Future (BRF) will use the ship to haul up to 13,250 deadweight tonnes (DWT) across the 230 nautical miles (or about 265, as the crow flies) between the ports at Brønnøy and Elnesvågen without burning a drop of diesel.

“It’s going to run back and forth, back and forth, just like a ferry,” explains Oivind Berge, co-owner of Berge Rederi Future, in a TradeWinds interview. He added that the round trip takes around 24 hours, with charging facilities installed at the loading and discharge ports. “Then we can go back and forth continuously.”.

The 130M vessel BRF Froan left the shipyard at Jiangsu SOHO Marine Heavy Industry, in China last week, and is currently en route to Norway where it is set to begin shipping huge chunks of marble early next year.

The ship’s massive battery sends electrons to a 6,000 kW (about 8,000 hp) electric motors that turn the propellers. How that works is obvious – what might be less obvious is what those big stovepipe deals at the back of the BRF Froan are.

Those are called rotor, or rotary sails, and they one-up the old-school version by using something call the Magnus effect to produce forward thrust. Basically, as the tall cylinders spin, the wind flowing around them creates a pressure difference that generates lift perpendicular to the wind. That lift produces forward thrust, helping push the ship along and reducing the amount of electricity it needs to draw from its batteries once under way.

The tech giant estimates the two rotary sails will save about 339 kW per trip, while the switch to battery power will save another 10,000 tons of harmful carbon emissions and 220 tons of nitrous oxides each year.

Recent findings suggest that interesting Engineering is reporting the total cost of the project at approximately USD 52 million (NOK 500 million). A second vessel, named BRF Frøya, is already under construction in China and is scheduled for delivery in 2027.

#155448. Pay Now, Save Later: Why It Makes Sense to Buy a More Expensive Old Car

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (740 w)
📖 Baca
EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Roadandtrack ↗ Open Full Page

Pay Now, Save Later: Why It Makes Sense to Buy a More Expensive Old Car

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (740 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Roadandtrack

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that one of the problems with the classic end of the automotive hobby is that everyone wants a clean car.
  • This story originally appeared in Volume 38 of Road & Track.
  • Why would you buy something with obvious complications?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that one of the problems with the classic end of the automotive hobby is that everyone wants a clean car. Whether your goal is to keep it that way, preserve and use it, or modify it to suit your tastes, the road will be a whole lot smoother if you start from a healthy place. Trust me, buying a good example of an older car is better for your health. I’ve been there.

This story originally appeared in Volume 38 of Road & Track.

Why would you buy something with obvious complications? To save money, right? But guess what—you’re undervaluing your own time, and, except for a few rare occasions, the savings never materialize. Trying to fix up a bad car without already being an expert bad-car fixer is like trying to treat someone with a spinal injury without being a doctor: It’s going to be brutal, painful, and expensive in ways you can’t anticipate.

It has been revealed that A clean car has fewer unknowns. With a not-so-clean car, damage from accidents may not have been repaired to factory spec. Paintwork may not quite match. “Just a little bit of rust” is almost never an accurate assessment of that metal-eating menace. “You’re not going to believe what we found in here” will become your own sad catchphrase.

This is particularly true for Aughts-era cars because they are potentially usable for everyday driving. The fantasy of dailying something like a sweet E39 BMW M5 can run into the reality of owning a 20-something-year-old specialty product. You might be thinking: It’s not like buying an old Ford Woody and needing artisan-­level skills. Most Aughts cars should be reliable enough to drive regularly at freeway speeds. The worst that could happen is I might need to replace a few still readily available parts, right? Maybe. Maybe not. You’ll quickly find out which local shops won’t touch cars that are over 10 years old.

It has been revealed that now, if I were a talented hobbyist mechanic, or a professional one, I could probably spot a deal where my skill set could be applied to a particular car’s needs, creating unique value for me. And yes, anyone could learn those skills with some time and effort. But do you want to spend your nights and weekends wrenching, not to customize your car but to repair it? Or do you want to spend that time driving?

According to recent reports, for everyone who does not fix cars for a hobby and wants a cool car to drive for fun and maybe modify a bit: Get the clean car. Time is money, and if your money has to buy professional time un-shitboxing a previous owner’s mistakes, it’s going to cost you both dollars and days. You’re not just losing what you may have saved on the purchase price in repairs but also paying in the lost opportunity of a car that’s not on the road being enjoyed.

One of my recent purchases is an old Mercedes that I am having professionals modify for me. The ­difference between a great and a rough example of this car is about $15,000. Real money, but to make a bad example into a good one would be more than ­double that figure.

According to recent reports, so yeah, you pay more on the way in. But guess what? When you go to sell it, you’re on the other end of the same equation. Money out, money in. Because everybody wants the clean example, and you’re ­holding the goods.

Wit more than sixty (60!) upcoming-energy models spanning everything from driverless excavators to cabless loaders and hybrid-electric mining trucks, the next generation of Zoomlion machinery is wowing everyone at bauma 2026.

Closing out a breakout year for the Chinese equipment brand, Zoomlion arrived at bauma China 2026 with more than 60 intelligent, new-energy heavy equipment options spanning eight product categories, highlighting both the company’s manufacturing prowess and establishing it as a leader in what it’s calling, “physical AI.”.

And, while the company brought along a few examples of the Z01 and Z03 humanoid robots that are presently building a new equipment asset every six minutes, the real headliner was the cabless Zoomlion excavator robot shown, above.

Zoomlion says its proprietary RobotOps embodied AI operating system built around a vision-language-action (VLA) model that uses a comprehensive suite of sensors to give it “a 540-degree view” of the world around it.

Basically marketing-speak for, “better than just 360 degree camera views,” the sensors helps the Zoomlion machine correctly identify objects in a variety of conditions, determining their positions, orientations, and dimensions, then using the company’s Zbrain platform to translate that information into physical machine movements – and those movements are “just” being calculated for the excavator.

That 540-degree 3D vision system gives the autonomous excavator a much more complete picture of its surroundings, using multiple sensors to identify obstacles, understand distances, and navigate a constantly changing worksite.

The manufacturer indicates its intelligent Zbrain platform has been trained on millions of hours of operational data and tens of thousands of real-world scenarios, and allows Zoomlion’s autonomous machines to interpret natural-language job instructions, autonomously deconstructing complex tasks into simple step-by-step workflows before scanning the surrounding terrain, classifying the materials, and determining the right digging and gripping paths to deliver fully automate excavation, loading, slope dressing, brick paving, or material handling.

The bipedal humanoid Z01 robots will be at the show to guide visitors through the sprawling Zoomlion display, and will reportedly be using facial and gesture recognition to identify and remember individuals, while executing force-compliant motion planning and real-time obstacle avoidance to perform interactive gestures such as fist bumps and waves.

You can check out some photos of Zoomlion’s roboticized and electrified equipment display, below, then let us know what you think about someone else‘s claims about their AI and robotic sleadership status in the comments.

Industry News: A Used Cybertruck Is Selling A Month Faster Than A Ford F-150

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (681 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Insideevs

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, if you had to guess which used pickup found a buyer fastest in October, the Toyota Tacoma would be a sensible bet.
  • Industry observers note that the data from the latest iSeeCars study covers 1.1 million used vehicles that changed hands in October, so this was before Tesla declared it would discontinue the Cybertruck in 2027.
  • The Cybertruck surpassed all other pickups, averaging 39.1 days, compared to 65.5 days for used pickups overall.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, if you had to guess which used pickup found a buyer fastest in October, the Toyota Tacoma would be a sensible bet. It’s America’s best-selling midsize truck and has a reputation for holding its value. Or you might pick the super frugal Ford Maverick Hybrid. But the truck that beat them both was the Tesla Cybertruck.

Industry observers note that the data from the latest iSeeCars study covers 1.1 million used vehicles that changed hands in October, so this was before Tesla declared it would discontinue the Cybertruck in 2027. The study looked at one- to five-year-old vehicles and ranked models by how long they’d been listed before selling.

The Cybertruck surpassed all other pickups, averaging 39.1 days, compared to 65.5 days for used pickups overall. The Maverick Hybrid came closest at 43.3 days, followed by the Rivian R1T at 45.2 and the F-150 Lightning at 47.4. The Tacoma came in fifth position.

According to recent reports, the gap between the two electric pickups at either end of the list was even more striking. A used Chevrolet Silverado EV took 107.5 days to sell, putting it last among the 24 trucks in the study. That’s a 68-day difference between two American electric pickups. Across the wider used market, EVs averaged about 46 days to find a buyer, around nine fewer than hybrids and 15 fewer than gas vehicles.

Sources indicate that how promptly a used Cybertruck sold seems to have changed a lot since May 2024, when some sellers were cutting as much as $30,000 from their asking prices after listing their trucks for close to $200,000. By December of that year, we reported that used Cybertrucks were piling up on dealer lots, with data at the time showing they stayed for 75 days, up from 27 in May.

Sources indicate that then owners got a look at what Tesla itself would pay for a used Cybertruck trade-in. One year later, in May 2025, one owner of a $99,990 dual-motor Foundation Series truck got a trade-in estimate of $65,400 after driving it just 6,211 miles.

So even though the Cybertruck was the fastest-selling used pickup in iSeeCars’ newly introduced study, it didn’t report what buyers paid, so we don’t know whether owners got their asking price or had to lower it to sell.

Tesla will build the last Cybertrucks at the end of summer 2027, and this will reshape their used market. Elon Musk originally confirmed production would end around the middle of the year, but then extended the run to fill more orders. And if you order a Cybertruck now, the only one you can get is the $110,000 tri-motor Cyberbeast, so anyone who wants a less expensive dual-motor truck has to look for a used example.

It has been revealed that once the last fresh Cybertruck is sold, I’d expect collectors and everyday truck buyers to look at used ones differently. Someone after a clean Foundation Series truck with low miles might pay a little extra for one close to home, especially since it could be months before another comes up for sale nearby.

At the same time, someone who just needs an electric pickup to tow a trailer has more options. If a used dual-motor Cybertruck costs about the same as a Ford F-150 Lightning or a Rivian R1T, I suspect that buyer will care more about mileage, condition, and how much battery warranty is left than when Tesla built its last truck.
