📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that I recently spent some time driving a 2026 Chevy Blazer EV SS, and the experience got me thinking about where Chevy’s electric family hot rod fits in the history of SS-badged machines.
  • Sources indicate that I am a self-appointed expert on which SS models rocked, and which ones should have been an RS at best (in high school, we all knew RS stood for Really Slow).
  • I drove a Camaro SS 1LE at Carolina Motorsports Park for our How Fast Does Your Car Have to Be to Outrun a Cop?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that I recently spent some time driving a 2026 Chevy Blazer EV SS, and the experience got me thinking about where Chevy’s electric family hot rod fits in the history of SS-badged machines. Chevy established the Super Sport trim in the 1960s with some legendary cars (Impala, Chevelle, Camaro, Nova) and then applied it scattershot over the decades, with some latter-day SS models worthy of the heritage and others an exercise in credibility dilution.

Sources indicate that I am a self-appointed expert on which SS models rocked, and which ones should have been an RS at best (in high school, we all knew RS stood for Really Slow). So here are my SS rankings, grouped by Worthy of the Name and Should Have Been an RS. Fun fact: One SS was both.

I drove a Camaro SS 1LE at Carolina Motorsports Park for our How Fast Does Your Car Have to Be to Outrun a Cop? story. Our cop-evading candidates also included a Ferrari 488 GTB, and while the Ferrari was the quickest car of the day, the Camaro wasn’t as far behind as you might expect. It’s also possible that I just felt more comfortable pushing a Camaro than I did a Ferrari, but the SS 1LE remains the track-rat bargain of this century. I still want one.

See all results for newly introduced 2026 Chevrolet Blazer for sale near 02128.

Sources indicate that one of my high school hobbies was cadging test drives at car dealerships. Maybe I should have felt bad about wasting dealers’ time, but on some level I believed that I might actually buy whatever car I was begging for a drive. And I was arriving in my IROC, which was presentable enough to imply at least some trade-in value. I drove plenty of cars—the second-generation Ford Probe GT with its frisky V-6 was a pleasant surprise—but I did get shut down whenever I exceeded the threshold of deal-signing plausibility that was assigned when I rolled onto a given lot. That’s what happened when I asked to drive a 1994 Impala SS that was in the showroom of a local car dealer. I vividly remember what the salesman told me: “If everyone drives it, nobody buys it.” Instead, he gave me the keys to a Monte Carlo SS. I was amazed that a car with a similar engine to mine (the ubiquitous Chevy 5.0) could be so much slower. “Someday, I’ll write a story about how not all Chevys deserve an SS badge,” I probably didn’t say. But let’s imagine I did. What a perceptive lad!

It has been revealed that I still haven’t driven a bubble-Caprice Impala SS. But I continue to revere them. They’re like a cop car, but cooler!

Sources indicate that speaking of cop-cars-but-cooler, the Chevy SS was the civilian version of the contemporary Caprice, and it was like Chevy’s version of an E39 BMW M5, complete with 415 horsepower and an available manual transmission. Of course, just right is never enough, so we had Lingenfelter Performance Engineering bolt on a supercharger before I took an SS on a multi-state investigation of the history of bootlegging. Sliding that car around on dirt roads out in moonshine country was so much fun I almost forgot I had a job to do. Which may or may not have involved bringing some things in the trunk back to Michigan. I get amnesia when I try to recall any details about that, but the SS—that I remember, and fondly. If you want one, maybe don’t wait too long, because the SS secret is out, based on what I see lurking on Bring a Trailer.

See all results for latest 2026 Chevrolet Blazer for sale near 02128.

Sources indicate that I’ve never driven a Chevelle SS, but when we had one in a comparison test, it sounded like it was a royal handful. A 13.81-second quarter-mile at 102 mph isn’t super quick now, but consider that the first 500 feet of that run was probably devoted to wheelspin management as the 7.4-liter, 450-hp (gross-rated) V-8 abused the primitive tires of the day.

Of the Chevelle’s brakes, Sam Posey remarked, “While they’re working, they are predicta­ble.”.

The Cobalt SS was a sneaky performance car when it debuted with a supercharged, 205-hp four-cylinder in 2005, and later got a 260-hp turbocharged upgrade. Chevy also built it in naturally aspirated form (hold that thought). This was around the time when GM started to figure out the concept of handling, and the Cobalt SS’s excellent all-around performance prompted me to conjure an unlikely contest in 2006. The premise: I race against Dale Earnhardt, Jr., around a tight road course at the Charlotte Motor Speedway infield. He’d get a Cobalt SS. And I’d get a 505-hp Corvette Z06. I beat him, but not for his lack of trying—he pushed that Cobalt so hard he pitted in with gravel falling out of the left-rear wheel because his track-out lines were starting to include real estate beyond the actual track.

Then we went Corvette to Corvette, and that went how you’d expect, as evidenced by his note in my Z06 press kit: “Good luck next time. Dale Jr., 30.8 (you 32.2).”.

Dropping a dang Corvette engine in a family SUV is usually the sort of procedure that requires an engine hoist, a wrecked C4, and a long weekend. But in 2006 Chevy did that deed at the factory, giving us the Trailblazer SS, a 395-hp SUV that hit 60 mph in 5.5 seconds and conjured the casual menace of the ‘90s Impala SS. It also had upgraded brakes and suspension, modifications that our John Phillips described as “comprehensively testosteronated”. If you like the whole Trailblazer SS deal but wish it were weirder, GM also built a Saab version, the 9-7X Aero. It was about as Swedish as apple pie at a baseball game on the Fourth of July, and remains the most powerful Saab I can think of at the moment.

OK, the stopwatch doesn’t lie: the Blazer EV SS destroys its predecessors at the drag strip. The trip to 60 mph is over in 3.3 seconds, and the quarter-mile requires just 11.8 seconds. That beats an automatic 2019 Camaro SS (3.9 and 12.2 seconds for those respective runs), which itself was slightly quicker than the manual Camaro SSs we tested. On power alone—615 horsepower and 650 pound-feet of torque—the electric Blazer deserves entry to the SS club.

Sources indicate that in other ways, it’s merely casually sporty, but that’s been the SS mien in a lot of cases. I appreciate that you can get it in habanero orange, an extroverted hue that caused one of my kids to mistake it for a Lamborghini Urus for about 50 milliseconds. And, in this age of inflation, the $395 performance package is a huge bargain for the upgrades it brings: 22-inch summer tires and high-friction brake pads and rotors. Those front rotors are 15.3 inches and are grabbed by six-piston Brembo calipers. That’s legit hardware, as evidenced by its 157-foot stop from 60 mph.

It has been revealed that the Blazer EV SS interior gives you some SS branding on the seats and steering wheel but otherwise looks mostly like any other Blazer EV, which is to say mostly like any other Chevy SUV. Which is fine. If I were the person at GM in charge of cost-benefit analysis, I too would opt for cruddy lower door plastic as long as I got to keep Super Cruise.

The Blazer EV SS is worthy of the SS badge. Whether it’s worthy of the Blazer one is a different discussion that you can continue on your forum, K5 Freaks 4EVR.

In a recent development, the positive news here was that Chevy brought back a V-8-powered Impala SS that was good at doing burnouts. The bad news was that it could barely avoid doing burnouts at all times because it was front-wheel-drive. Yes, Chevy dropped a dang 303-hp LS engine in the front-drive Impala of the day, resulting in torque steer that made every ditch a possibility. Our own Tony Quiroga described that Impala SS as a car that “gives the feeling that it’s waging war with itself”. Other observations from that review:.

-“Keeping an 18-year-old platform competitive is not an insubstantial task.”.

-“Dive, squat, and roll control could be described as nautical.”.

-On the skidpad, “The Impala leaned over far enough to be included in Who's Who in Body Roll.”.

-“Impressed by the 154-mph top speed? Driving the SS at that speed is scary enough to be a stunt on NBC's Fear Factor.”.

-“The front-strut suspension crashes over pavement imperfections as if someone had overlooked the advantages of bushings.”.

According to recent reports, at the time, my wife had an Impala as a company car. She was a pharma sales rep for Johnson & Johnson, and her trunk was always full of Tylenol PM and K-Y Jelly. It would have been funny if she ever got pulled over and searched. Also, the second “A” of the trunk badge fell off, so we fondly referred to her car as the Impal. That was the right assignment for that era of Impala.

In a recent development, during the early-2000s hot-truck heyday, there were some wicked creations. Ford said, “Let’s put a 380-hp supercharged V-8 in a regular-cab two-wheel-drive F-150, call it the Lightning and do some huge burnouts.” Over at Dodge, they said, “Let’s drop a 500-hp Viper V-10 in a regular-cab, two-wheel-drive Ram, call it the SRT-10 and do some even huger burnouts.” When Chevy got in on the game, it said, “Let’s build a Silverado with an extended cab, all-wheel-drive, and 345 hp. We’ll call it the SS, and it won’t do burnouts.” Eventually Chevy built a rear-drive version, but the Silverado SS still got noogies and purple nurples at recess from the Dodge and Ford.

According to recent reports, we stated the Maxx itself was “a runty-looking cross between a family sedan and an ice chest,” and the SS treatment didn’t do a whole lot to energize that off-putting shape. The Maxx SS was powered by an iron-block pushrod V-6 that made all of 240 horsepower, sloshed to the front wheels by a four-speed automatic. It hit 60 mph in 6.9 seconds and topped out at a governed 115 mph. This Malibu Maxx didn’t need to be called an SS. In fact, this Malibu Maxx didn’t need to be at all. It reminded me of when I bought reflective mailbox lettering decals and made my parents’ rusty 1989 Subaru DL wagon the DL SS.

In a recent development, how is the Cobalt SS on both the worthy list and the SS trash pile? Because for two years, Chevy offered a naturally aspirated version that wheezed out just 170 horsepower. (The good version was formally named the Cobalt SS Supercharged.) Chevy itself got embarrassed by this SS’s half-heartedness and renamed it the Cobalt Sport after two years, proving that even pre-bankruptcy GM had limits to its cynicism. Happily, no subsequent SS stooped to that level, and hopefully none ever will.

Recent findings suggest that ezra Dyer is a Car and Driver senior editor and columnist. He's now based in North Carolina but still remembers how to turn right. He owns a 2009 GEM e4 and once drove 206 mph. Those facts are mutually exclusive.

Mice slept 70% less after scientists switched off these brain cells

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (880 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Why does being awake for too long make us increasingly desperate for sleep?
  • It has been revealed that the longer we go without sleep, the more difficult it becomes to stay awake.
  • In a recent development, researchers led by Professor Alex Schier at the Biozentrum, University of Basel, have now identified brain cells that help regulate this process.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Why does being awake for too long make us increasingly desperate for sleep? Scientists at the University of Basel in Switzerland have identified two groups of brain cells in mice that become more active the longer the animals remain awake. These neurons play a critical role in creating the pressure to sleep, offering newly introduced clues about how the brain regulates our need for rest.

It has been revealed that the longer we go without sleep, the more difficult it becomes to stay awake. This buildup of sleep pressure, often called sleep drive, helps ensure that extended periods of wakefulness are followed by longer and deeper sleep. Although sleep is essential for survival, exactly how the brain measures time spent awake and converts that information into an increasing need for sleep has remained a mystery.

In a recent development, researchers led by Professor Alex Schier at the Biozentrum, University of Basel, have now identified brain cells that help regulate this process. The work was conducted in collaboration with scientists from Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center and Auburn University.

Recent findings suggest that "We have identified neuronal populations that monitor prolonged wakefulness and actively promote sleep," states Alex Schier. "This is an important missing piece of the puzzle in understanding why we become sleepy.".

Scientists Identify Brain Cells That Drive Sleep Pressure.

According to recent reports, to investigate how sleep pressure develops, the team studied patterns of brain activity in mice under three different conditions: normal cycles of sleeping and waking, extended sleep deprivation, and recovery sleep. By comparing these patterns, they identified brain regions whose activity changed according to how long the animals had been awake.

Industry observers note that within one of these regions, the brainstem, researchers pinpointed two groups of neurons involved in controlling sleep drive. Known as GABAergic and serotonergic neurons, both groups became progressively more active as the mice remained awake. Their activity then decreased once the animals fell asleep.

The next question was whether these neurons simply tracked how long the mice had been awake or actually helped create the growing need for sleep.

Experiments revealed that the neurons were directly involved in driving sleep. When researchers artificially activated both groups, the mice slept longer and more deeply, showing the same type of recovery sleep normally seen after extended wakefulness. When the neurons were inhibited, however, the animals slept substantially less and were able to remain awake and alert.

"These neurons do not simply signal that an animal has been awake," says Schier. "Our experiments show that they are crucial to promote sleep, and that they may be key components of the neural circuitry that generates sleep drive.".

In a recent development, the results provide particularly strong evidence that certain neurons activated during wakefulness do more than register lost sleep. They actively help generate the pressure that eventually pushes the brain toward sleep.

Mice Sleep 70% Less When Key Neurons Are Inhibited.

Industry observers note that further experiments produced an especially surprising result. When scientists suppressed both groups of neurons for an extended period, the mice slept approximately 70% less than normal.

According to recent reports, even more unexpectedly, most of these animals did not display some of the serious behavioral problems typically associated with prolonged sleep deprivation. Despite getting dramatically less sleep, many avoided impairments that researchers would ordinarily expect.

These findings suggest that the identified neurons influence not only the amount of time animals spend sleeping, but also how strongly the pressure to sleep increases during wakefulness.

Rather than simply responding to exhaustion, the brain appears to use specific neural circuits to actively regulate the growing need for rest.

A New Direction for Sleep Research.

In a recent development, understanding these circuits could open notable new avenues for studying sleep and its effects on the body. Researchers now hope to determine how the identified neurons communicate with other brain regions and what molecular processes allow them to generate sleep pressure.

Sources indicate that "Future studies could reveal how these neurons interact with the rest of the brain, and how sleep drive is generated at the molecular level," notes Dr. William Joo, first author of the study. "Our ability to stably transform sleep behavior also allows us to explore adaptations to long-term sleep loss - this may eventually reveal ways to confer resilience to sleep deprivation and other physiological challenges.".

The findings establish that GABAergic and serotonergic neurons in the brainstem become increasingly active during prolonged wakefulness and play an essential role in promoting sleep.

Industry observers note that determining exactly how the brain makes sleep increasingly difficult to resist remains a major objective of sleep research. Beyond improving scientists' understanding of sleep disorders, this discovery could help explain how the nervous system adapts to extended wakefulness and other physical challenges.

Ultimately, a clearer understanding of the brain circuits responsible for sleep pressure could inspire upcoming treatments and potentially reveal ways to improve resilience to sleep deprivation.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the industry's in a troubling position right now.
  • According to recent reports, chris Wilson, former lead designer on Path of Exile and co-founder of Grinding Gear Games, discussed the merits of Larian's approach with Destin on YouTube.
  • Sources indicate that "They made it, they had a good extended early access period for getting feedback without spoiling the game, and they released it in a sincere way," he explains.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the industry's in a troubling position right now. Layoffs are widespread, triple-A budgets have ballooned, and it seems harder than ever to know what'll make a game stick. In the mind of one of the central devs on the Path of Exile series, Baldur's Gate 3 is a strong example of the kind of business model studios should aspire toward.

According to recent reports, chris Wilson, former lead designer on Path of Exile and co-founder of Grinding Gear Games, discussed the merits of Larian's approach with Destin on YouTube. "A like Baldur's Gate 3 is a great example of a very true game," he indicates.

Sources indicate that "They made it, they had a good extended early access period for getting feedback without spoiling the game, and they released it in a sincere way," he explains. "Then, when given the opportunity to do more stuff for it, they noted, actually, we want to make something else. That's cool, they'll make another thing, and that'll do well.".

According to recent reports, to his perception, "there's no manipulation there." Larian "got rewarded" appropriately and "everyone had a good time" in that transaction. "Sure, it's because it's an exceptionally good game," he adds. "But I think that a shift back to making games [like that] - it's less complicated, you can make more story-driven games. It doesn't have to be that everything is a live-service.".

Sources indicate that that's the million-dollar principle, really. Many games at the triple-A level simply don't need these features or mechanics, and Baldur's Gate 3 proves you can still have a close-to-one-to-one transaction between you and the player and be hugely successful.

Industry observers note that clair Obscur: Expedition 33 and the Final Fantasy 7 remake trilogy are further examples. Wilson admits he probably wouldn't have made Path of Exile if they couldn't do it with live-service aspects, but that's because they were integral to the vision.

"It's designed around a substantial economy with lots of players, which is why it's free-to-play," he notes. "It was very much designed to be live-service from the start.".

Weekly digests, tales from the communities you love, and more.

The current problem is games are being released with online elements "because the spreadsheet indicates it'll make more money," and the game is "contorted out of its single-player true experience" to facilitate these elements.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the Sims 4 developers recently promised an exciting year for the game, and the franchise as a whole, and we just got an early look at one of those first events.
  • Royalty & Legacy’s first trailer debuted on Thursday, revealing a February 12 release date, and showing off the expansion for the first time.
  • Recent findings suggest that there’s a lot going on in Royalty & Legacy, which is priced $40.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the Sims 4 developers recently promised an exciting year for the game, and the franchise as a whole, and we just got an early look at one of those first events. After some light teasing, the developer unveiled Royalty & Legacy, the game’s next expansion.

Royalty & Legacy’s first trailer debuted on Thursday, revealing a February 12 release date, and showing off the expansion for the first time.

Recent findings suggest that there’s a lot going on in Royalty & Legacy, which is priced $40. For one, it introduces a upcoming world, Ondarion, which is going to be the setting for your kingdom, as you join a race for the throne. The expansion introduces Dynasty and Nobility - two new systems you can use to create your own world of royal shenanigans.

Ondarion is made up of three neighborhoods (regions). Each region has a unique theme and culture, and they’re each ruled by a Dynasty. Dambele is a place that prioritises art and community. Verdemar is a chaotic world of outlaws and nobles. Finally, Bellacorde is an extravagant region known for opulence and romance.

Speaking of building places, Royalty & Legacy also adds a new Lot type, The Backroom Lot. It serves two functions that change with the time of day. For instance, it can be a library or gym in the morning, and shift into a night club at night. Dambele has its own library-turned-rave, for instance.

According to recent reports, at the heart of Ondarion are all the possible fantasy lives and stories you can live. The Sims calls them Powershifts, and they include some well-known Arthurian fantasies and other, more silly ones.

Swordsmanship is the new 10-level skill arriving with the expansion, which further plays into those fantasies by letting your Sims duel. There are even Swordsmanship Tournaments you can watch take place across every neighborhood in Ondarion.

Then there are Secret Passageways, which let you speed up moving across the upcoming regions. They essentially let your Sims teleport between designated passageways, either on their own lots, or other lots in the world. Some of these are hidden for you to find, while others you can create.

In terms of new careers, there’s the Noble Career, where your Sim can rise through several Noble Rankings by doing basically what nobles had to do in the middle ages to earn favour.

It has been revealed that the aforementioned Dynasty System is how you can join any of Ondarion’s existing families, or start your own. You actually have a lot of say in what goes on, including the usual business of appointing heirs.

It has been revealed that of course, no royal roleplay would be complete without scandals, which is where the Scandals System comes in. Through it, you can create stories to discredit others, or even topple an entire dynasty.

In November, you may recall The Sims 4 introducing new free items inspired by West African culture. In creating that content, EA worked with a group of Simmers who have direct ties to West African countries.

The group’s guidance was once again utilised to build the Dambele neighborhood in this expansion, and some of the lots around the world of Ondarion were even created by members of the group.

Industry observers note that while you wait for Royalty & Legacy to actually arrive, there’s more in The Sims 4 you can jump in right now. The game recently kicked off a collaboration with fashion brand Coach that brought several free items to Create a Sim, and Build Buy. That arrived alongside a free update, which already makes for a busy start of the year for The Sims 4.

Latest Update: America is building just 10% of the power lines it needs, experts warn

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1150 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • America's electricity needs are growing rapidly, but the nation's aging power grid is struggling to keep up.
  • In a Policy Forum paper published in Science, energy policy researchers from Carnegie Mellon University and the University of California San Diego warn that the United States faces one of the world's most serious bottlenecks in electricity transmission.
  • America Is Building Just 10% of the Power Lines It Needs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

America's electricity needs are growing rapidly, but the nation's aging power grid is struggling to keep up. More electric vehicles, increased electricity use in heavy industry, and the explosive growth of data centers are driving demand higher, putting additional pressure on an infrastructure system that is already falling behind.

In a Policy Forum paper published in Science, energy policy researchers from Carnegie Mellon University and the University of California San Diego warn that the United States faces one of the world's most serious bottlenecks in electricity transmission. The problem could have major consequences for electricity prices, grid reliability, and the nation's economic future.

America Is Building Just 10% of the Power Lines It Needs.

A major concern is the extremely slow pace of transmission construction. Over the past five years, the continental United States has added an average of only about 500 miles of high-voltage transmission lines annually. Research suggests the country needs approximately 5,000 miles each year to triple the size of its interregional transmission network by 2050 and accommodate future electricity demand.

That means the U.S. is building new high-voltage transmission lines at just one-tenth of the estimated pace needed.

Sources indicate that high-voltage transmission lines serve as the highways of the electricity system, carrying large amounts of power over long distances from generating facilities to communities and businesses. Connecting regional grids allows electricity to flow more easily between areas, helping balance supply and demand when local power production falls short.

Studies have shown that larger, better-connected electricity networks can reduce costs for consumers while also lowering the risk of catastrophic blackouts. When one region experiences a power shortage, electricity from another region can help keep the lights on.

Despite these advantages, expanding the nation's transmission infrastructure has proved extraordinarily difficult.

The Biggest Obstacle Isn't Technology.

According to the researchers (Madeline Yozwiak, David G. Victor, and M. Granger Morgan), the main barriers to modernizing America's power grid are political and regulatory rather than technological.

According to recent reports, responsibility for approving major transmission projects is divided among federal agencies, state governments, local authorities, and private companies. Each has its own priorities and interests, creating numerous opportunities for proposed power lines to be delayed or blocked.

Existing electric utilities can also have financial reasons to resist stronger connections between regions. Greater competition from electricity suppliers elsewhere could weaken their influence over local markets, reducing the incentive to support projects that would benefit the broader electricity system.

As a result, even transmission projects that could lower costs and improve reliability across the country can struggle to gain approval.

Three Ways to Fix America's Power Grid Crisis.

To address the growing shortfall, the researchers recommend a three-part strategy combining stronger government action, modern transmission technologies, international cooperation, and regulatory reform.

1. Make better use of existing federal powers and advanced technologies.

It has been revealed that the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) and the Department of Energy (DOE) already have legal authorities that could help move important transmission projects forward. The researchers argue that these agencies should use those powers more effectively, including identifying transmission corridors of national importance and addressing disputes that prevent projects from receiving state-level approval.

It has been revealed that technological improvements could also dramatically increase the amount of electricity the grid can carry. One approach, known as reconductoring, involves replacing existing power line conductors with more advanced materials capable of transmitting more electricity without necessarily requiring entirely new routes.

Other advances, including newer High-Voltage Direct Current (VSC-HVDC) systems, offer additional ways to move large amounts of electricity efficiently. The researchers suggest that modern transmission technologies could double or even triple capacity.

Sources indicate that underground high-voltage direct current (HVDC) cables offer another promising option. These systems can carry substantial amounts of electricity over long distances and could potentially be installed along existing highways and railroad corridors. Using these established routes could help avoid some of the land-use disputes and approval challenges that often delay conventional transmission projects.

2. Learn from countries that have already overcome similar obstacles.

The United States trails several international counterparts in building long-distance HVDC infrastructure and coordinating electricity transmission across regional and national boundaries.

Other countries have demonstrated that large transmission projects can move forward despite complicated political approval processes. Some have also successfully deployed underground HVDC systems on a large scale.

According to recent reports, rather than developing every solution independently, the researchers suggest that the U.S. should study these international experiences and adapt approaches that have already proved successful.

According to recent reports, one proposal is to establish an international forum involving electricity regulators and other experts, potentially led by organizations such as the National Association of Regulatory Utility Commissioners (NARUC). Such a forum could help American policymakers identify effective regulatory practices, planning strategies, and technologies used elsewhere.

Recent findings suggest that 3. Create a national commission to break the political deadlock.

The researchers also recommend establishing a Presidential-Congressional Transmission Commission to address the political and regulatory conflicts that have slowed grid expansion for decades.

Modeled on previous successful bipartisan commissions, the proposed group would bring together key stakeholders to negotiate difficult decisions and develop a coordinated plan for reform.

Its responsibilities would include recommending changes to state and federal laws, examining whether FERC should receive broader authority over the locations of new transmission projects, and developing financial incentives for companies that lead new construction.

The commission could also recommend financial rewards for communities that host transmission infrastructure, helping ensure that local residents share in the benefits of projects that serve larger regions.

Why America's Power Grid Crisis Could Get Worse.

In a recent development, the researchers emphasize that the underlying challenge is not a lack of engineering solutions. Instead, the country's divided decision-making system allows individual stakeholders to obstruct projects that could deliver substantial nationwide benefits.

"The fundamental challenge isn't technical, it's jurisdictional. Authority is divided among federal, state, and private entities, each with distinct priorities. When every stakeholder possesses the power to say no, even high-value projects that benefit the entire nation struggle to move forward," the authors warn.

Their assessment suggests that simply continuing with the existing system of overlapping regulations and fragmented authority will not be enough to meet America's growing electricity needs.

Without meaningful changes to how transmission projects are planned, approved, and built, the United States risks a prolonged infrastructure shortfall. The researchers warn that failing to resolve these problems could weaken electricity reliability and inflict lasting damage on the national economy, even as demand for power continues to climb.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A latest set of Nintendo patents has been discovered that have paved the way for DS, 3DS, and Wii U games to return on Switch 2, so long as the player doesn’t mind shelling out for extra hardware.
  • It has been revealed that the Nintendo DS was a massively popular system, selling 154 million units worldwide.
  • One possible solution to Nintendo’s second screen problem may have been revealed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A latest set of Nintendo patents has been discovered that have paved the way for DS, 3DS, and Wii U games to return on Switch 2, so long as the player doesn’t mind shelling out for extra hardware.

It has been revealed that the Nintendo DS was a massively popular system, selling 154 million units worldwide. However, the system’s dual-screen design has made it hard for its titles to be rereleased on modern systems. Konami managed it with the Castlevania series, but few other companies seem interested in reviving their DS games on the Switch or Switch 2.

One possible solution to Nintendo’s second screen problem may have been revealed. According to RetroDodo, two patents have been discovered that will allow the Nintendo Switch and Switch 2 to play games from the previous console generations.

According to recent reports, the first patent allows a game to be instantly transferred between two systems, while the second allows a different console to be used alongside one running a title, with the ability to use touchscreen controls. Taken together, these patents could emulate the Nintendo DS, 3DS, and Wii U GamePad.

The caveat is that it would require someone to own two Nintendo Switch 2 units, or one of each Switch console, to run old games. This would be fine in a household that owns both systems, but for those who don’t, it’s an expensive proposition just to be able to run DS, 3DS, and Wii U titles.

Recent findings suggest that this isn’t the first time Nintendo has brought dual-screen games to consoles; DS games were available on the Wii U, with the GamePad used as the bottom screen. This isn’t the most elegant of solutions, especially as it forces the player to keep switching perspective between screens, but it gets the job done.

The caveat to these patents is that it would require someone owning two Nintendo Switch 2 units, or one of each Switch console, to run old games.

Recent findings suggest that there’s also the question of what games fans would even want to play on such a setup. The obvious answer is the Pokémon games, as fans would crawl through broken glass for modern ports of Pokémon HeartGold & SoulSilver that don’t cost hundreds of dollars on eBay. However, considering Game Freak seems averse to making money, there are still easier-to-port Pokémon games that aren’t on the Switch 2, and the DS games would take a ton of work to revision.

The Wii U also doesn’t have much, since pretty much all its best games are already on the Switch, and they received updated ports over the console’s lifespan. Sure, it’d be cool for Nintendo Land to return, but no one’s lining up for Star Fox Zero. The Wii U was such a bomb that Nintendo is unlikely to bring up its ghost, even through a costly hardware expansion.

It has been revealed that the Nintendo 3DS had a stacked library of amazing games, but some of them would lose the system's big selling point: 3D visuals. Super Mario 3D Land was a tremendous game, but it requires playing in 3D to get the full effect, especially for its stage secrets. The lack of Streepass and Spotpass would also take away a lot of the extra functions present in Nintendo 3DS games.

It’s entirely possible that these Nintendo Switch 2 patents won’t come to anything. After all, companies patent ideas all the time that never get made. The ability to play DS, 3DS, and Wii U games on the Switch 2 would be incredible, but the price of entry might be a bit too high for most fans, even if the titles are released for free on Nintendo Switch Online.

In a recent development, the custom-van craze of the 1970s will no doubt be studied by future archaeologists, and maybe you’ll be able to find a Chevy with an airbrushed unicorn on its side in a museum someday. The vans of that era were rolling hangout spots, an extension of the hippie-friendly appeal of the Volkswagen Type 2 into the domestic market, and their broad sheetmetal sides were the perfect canvas for art of all kinds.

See all results for used cars for sale near 43230.

It has been revealed that you might expect a 1978 rock ’n’ roll tribute custom van to feature Led Zeppelin or maybe Foghat. However, there’s only one King of Rock ’n’ Roll, and even if Elvis had left the building by 1977, the creator of this van went all in on a rolling temple to their hero.

The exterior features porthole windows, a full-length airbrushed portrait of Elvis on both sides, musical notes, and record details. Out back, there's the King’s massively side-burned visage and his indisputable title “The King of Rock ’n’ Roll.” Chrome side pipes and five-spoke 15-inch chrome wheels finish out the look.

Powering this roving Graceland is a 350-cubic-inch small-block V-8 with a four-barrel Edelbrock carburetor. Power gets to the ground through a three-speed automatic transmission, and the odometer at the moment demonstrates 42K miles. The original artwork dates back to the early 1980s, and the vehicle was comprehensively refurbished in 2019.

And, in case you have to ask, yes, it’s got an eight-track player for a stereo. Break out your collection of Elvis’s greatest hits and get ready to go cruise on through the night. One for the money, two for the show, three to get ready, then go, van, go.

#155391. A simple metal is hiding a strange new form of magnetism

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1579 w)

A simple metal is hiding a strange new form of magnetism

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1579 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that A surprisingly simple metal has revealed an unusual form of magnetism that could open new possibilities for quantum technology.
  • It has been revealed that the material, known as europium silicide (EuSi), contains an intricate magnetic structure that influences how electrons move and how their spins are oriented.
  • Sources indicate that the discovery is particularly significant because EuSi is a relatively simple metallic compound.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that A surprisingly simple metal has revealed an unusual form of magnetism that could open new possibilities for quantum technology. Researchers have found compelling evidence of a rare magnetic state in which electrons behave in unexpected ways, even though the material produces no overall magnetization.

It has been revealed that the material, known as europium silicide (EuSi), contains an intricate magnetic structure that influences how electrons move and how their spins are oriented. This behavior is associated with a phenomenon called p-wave magnetism, an emerging area of research that could eventually help scientists develop new approaches to controlling electronic properties.

Sources indicate that the discovery is particularly significant because EuSi is a relatively simple metallic compound. Unlike many materials previously considered for studying this exotic form of magnetism, it offers researchers a practical way to investigate the underlying physics in detail.

An Unexpected Discovery in a Simple Metal.

According to recent reports, the research began about three years ago at the Max Planck Institute for Chemical Physics of Solids (MPI CPfS) in Dresden, Germany. Dr. Erjian Cheng successfully grew high-quality single crystals of EuSi, providing the material needed for detailed experiments.

Sources indicate that when researchers first examined the crystals using photoemission techniques, which probe the energies and behavior of electrons inside materials, they noticed something unexpected. The magnetic arrangement of the atoms had a remarkably strong influence on the electronic band structure, which describes the energy levels electrons can occupy and helps determine how a material conducts electricity.

That observation raised an intriguing possibility. Could this simple compound contain an unconventional form of magnetism in which the spin of an electron is connected to the direction it travels?

"When we first measured the electronic structure of EuSi, we were surprised by the exceptionally large effect of magnetism on the electrons," explains Cheng. "That observation led us to investigate whether this simple compound could host a much more unusual magnetic state. The combination of crystal growth, neutron scattering and spin-resolved spectroscopy now provides compelling evidence for p-wave magnetism.".

Answering that question required an international collaboration involving 38 scientists from 19 institutions. Participants included researchers from ShanghaiTech University, the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, the Max Planck Institute for the Physics of Complex Systems and Oak Ridge National Laboratory.

A Strange Form of Magnetism That Cancels Itself Out.

Ordinary magnets, such as those attached to refrigerators, typically rely on a magnetic arrangement called ferromagnetism. In these materials, many electron spins align in the same direction, producing an overall magnetic field.

According to recent reports, at temperatures between approximately 33 and 62 kelvin, the magnetic moments of its europium atoms organize themselves into a repeating spiral pattern. These temperatures correspond to roughly minus 400 to minus 348 degrees Fahrenheit.

It has been revealed that each europium atom has a substantial magnetic moment, but their orientations balance one another across the spiral. As a result, the material has no net magnetization in this magnetic phase.

Industry observers note that however, the absence of overall magnetization does not mean magnetism has stopped influencing the electrons. In fact, the researchers found that the spiral arrangement produces a highly unusual electronic structure.

In the proposed p-wave magnetic state, electrons traveling in opposite directions have opposite spin polarizations. Electron spin is a quantum property that gives electrons magnetic characteristics, although it should not be understood as an electron literally spinning like a tiny ball.

Sources indicate that the relationship between an electron's direction of motion and its spin is called an odd-parity spin texture. This means that reversing the electron's momentum also reverses the associated spin polarization.

Industry observers note that other materials can display spin-dependent energy differences because of a phenomenon known as spin-orbit coupling, which connects an electron's motion to its spin. In EuSi, however, the unusual spin structure appears to arise mainly from interactions between magnetic moments and the specific symmetry of their spiral arrangement.

Experiments Reveal Evidence of Rare P-Wave Magnetism.

To determine whether EuSi truly exhibits the predicted magnetic state, the scientists combined several sophisticated experimental methods with theoretical calculations.

First, they used neutron diffraction, a technique that reveals how atoms and magnetic moments are arranged inside a material. These measurements confirmed that the europium magnetic moments form a spiral structure with the symmetry required for p-wave magnetism.

Sources indicate that next, the researchers examined the material using angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy. This method measures the energies and momenta of electrons, allowing scientists to map the electronic structure.

Sources indicate that the results indicated that magnetic ordering substantially reorganizes the electron energy levels. In particular, the team observed magnetically driven energy separations exceeding 100 millielectronvolts, indicating an unusually strong influence of magnetism on electron behavior.

The most decisive evidence came from spin-resolved photoemission spectroscopy, which allowed the researchers to examine electron spin polarization directly.

In a recent development, they observed that the sign of the spin polarization changed across successive magnetic Brillouin zones. These zones are regions of momentum space used by physicists to describe how electrons behave within a repeating magnetic structure.

The team also found that spin polarization became much weaker near locations where theoretical calculations predicted the p-wave spin texture should disappear.

Taken together, the measurements provide compelling experimental evidence consistent with the predicted p-wave magnetic state in EuSi.

A Hidden Magnetic Spiral With Two Different Orientations.

The researchers uncovered another unusual feature of EuSi involving chirality, a scientific term describing handedness.

Industry observers note that A familiar example is the difference between a left hand and a right hand. They are mirror images, but they cannot be perfectly superimposed.

Something similar happens with the magnetic spiral inside EuSi. Although the underlying crystal has a centrosymmetric structure, meaning its atomic arrangement is unchanged by inversion through a central point, the magnetic spiral can twist in either of two opposite directions.

These different spiral orientations create magnetic regions, or domains, with opposite handedness.

Using magnetic force microscopy and spatially resolved photoemission spectroscopy, the scientists identified domains measuring approximately ten micrometers across. For perspective, ten micrometers is about one-tenth the thickness of a typical human hair.

When the researchers examined these regions using circularly polarized light, they detected different electronic responses depending on the handedness of the magnetic spiral.

This finding demonstrates that the direction in which the magnetic structure twists is linked to the material's electronic properties.

Sources indicate that "What makes EuSi particularly exciting is that an unconventional electronic spin structure emerges from the magnetic order of a chemically simple metal," states Prof. Claudia Felser, Director at MPI CPfS. "This demonstrates how the discovery of latest materials can reveal entirely new electronic phenomena. EuSi now gives us an experimental platform to investigate how magnetic symmetry and chirality can be used to control electronic properties, with potential implications for future spintronics and unconventional superconductivity.".

Why This Discovery Matters for Quantum Technology.

One of the biggest challenges in studying p-wave magnetism has been finding materials that display the necessary magnetic properties while remaining practical for detailed experiments.

Earlier candidates have included insulating materials, as well as metals that develop the required magnetic order only at extremely low temperatures or have complicated symmetries that make their behavior difficult to interpret.

EuSi offers a particularly useful combination of characteristics.

It is a stoichiometric metal, meaning its constituent elements occur in a fixed chemical ratio. Researchers can also grow high-quality single crystals of the material, and its spiral magnetic arrangement has the symmetry associated with p-wave magnetism.

Together, these features make EuSi a promising experimental platform for exploring how exotic magnetic states influence the behavior of electrons.

Recent findings suggest that theoretical studies suggest that metallic p-wave magnets could display several remarkable properties. For example, they may allow electrons with particular spin orientations to carry electrical currents without requiring an external magnetic field.

They could also produce strong changes in spin polarization when an electric current is applied, potentially offering latest ways to manipulate electronic behavior.

These possibilities are especially relevant to spintronics, a field of technology that seeks to use electron spin, rather than electrical charge alone, to process and store information.

Another intriguing possibility involves unconventional superconductivity, in which electrical current flows without resistance through superconducting states that differ from those found in conventional superconductors.

Sources indicate that importantly, these predicted effects have not yet been demonstrated in EuSi. The discovery does not establish that the material can already perform these functions, but it gives researchers a promising system in which to test the predictions.

More broadly, the findings highlight how much of a material's behavior can remain hidden beneath an apparently simple chemical composition.

According to recent reports, A solid's properties depend on more than the elements it contains or how its atoms are positioned. The arrangement of magnetic moments, the symmetries they create, and the quantum behavior of electrons can also produce entirely unexpected effects.

By revealing compelling evidence of p-wave magnetism in EuSi, researchers have gained a new opportunity to investigate these relationships and explore how unusual magnetic structures might eventually be used to control the electronic properties of future materials.

Industry News: Gooseneck Hitches Explained

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, looking to tow a bigger and heavier trailer to carry the likes of livestock trailers, heavy equipment, or other vehicles?
  • This type of hitch gets its name from the high arch of steel that protrudes from the front end of the trailer.
  • According to recent reports, placing the mount right over the truck’s rear axle enables more of the accompanying trailer’s weight to push down on the tow vehicle’s rear end.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, looking to tow a bigger and heavier trailer to carry the likes of livestock trailers, heavy equipment, or other vehicles? Then you’re probably going to need a heavy-duty pickup truck that’s both capable of pulling such a hefty load and compatible with towing a gooseneck-style trailer hitch.

This type of hitch gets its name from the high arch of steel that protrudes from the front end of the trailer. Goosenecks are designed to clear a pickup truck’s tailgate and sides, since the ball hitch the trailer connects to sits squarely in the middle of the tow-vehicle’s bed.

According to recent reports, placing the mount right over the truck’s rear axle enables more of the accompanying trailer’s weight to push down on the tow vehicle’s rear end. The result? The combined truck and trailer benefit from greater stability once on the move.

In a recent development, fitting a gooseneck hitch to your truck is a completely different process relative to that of your typical rear-mounted hitch that hides under the bumper. You (or the manufacturer or service center) will need to drill right into the bed to install and mount the ball hitch and the accompanying safety chain attachment points.

See all results for used cars for sale near 21014.

According to recent reports, it’s a less invasive process than you may initially think, though. This is because the business end of a gooseneck is usually a long cylinder that sticks straight up from the bed.

It has been revealed that in theory, this setup is similar to that of a fifth wheel hitch. In reality, a fifth wheel hitch is a different beast. Notably, fifth wheel setups require a much bulkier kingpin and jaw-style bed-mounted hitch. This setup provides quieter operation and additional stability at speed relative to a gooseneck hitch, and is often used for the towing of recreational trailers designed for the likes of camping.

The ball mount and coupler of a gooseneck, however, make this the heartier hitch for towing heavy tonnage. We’re talking north of 30,000 pounds in some instances.

Credit the fact that a gooseneck hitch pushes a large amount of the trailer’s mass downward onto the truck’s rear end, which allows the trailer to better resist sway than if it were mounted to a conventional tow hitch. The hitch’s in-bed location also allows the truck to handle heavier loads.

Sources indicate that another benefit of the in-bed ball hitch is that it takes up far less space than a fifth wheel. This means a majority of the bed remains available for its intended purpose: hauling cargo.

So, what can you haul with a hitch that’s ready for gooseneck trailering duty? Well, there are about as many options as there are jobs on a worksite. The most flexible choice is a flatbed trailer, which can carry anything from secured payloads to heavy construction equipment. Other options include livestock carriers, dumping trailers, and car haulers.

See all results for used cars for sale near 21014.

Goosenecks also hold up well under abuse thanks to the tough but simple nature of the aforementioned ball hitch and coupler that connect the trailer and truck. It’s why gooseneck-style hitches are often used in agricultural and construction environments.

In a recent development, installation aside, a gooseneck hitch is a simpler and safer way to tow big loads without having to sacrifice much in the way of in-bed utility. Not everyone needs a gooseneck hitch to tow with, but those who do are sure to benefit from the extra capability this style of hitch provides.

Both hitch types are sturdy options for towing heavy loads, but gooseneck hitches, the strongest of which can handle more than 30,000 pounds of weight, are generally regarded as the more capable heavy-duty hitch.

Industry observers note that in theory, just about any pickup can be fitted with a gooseneck hitch. In practice, however, adding a gooseneck hitch to a light-duty pickup makes little sense given the lower payload and tow ratings of these trucks relative to their heavy-duty stablemates.

It has been revealed that the in-bed connection point between the ball and the coupler of a gooseneck effectively makes towing with this type of hitch safer than towing with a run-of-the-mill bumper-pull hitch—particularly when towing especially heavy loads. Credit the fact that gooseneck hitches put more of the trailer’s weight directly over the tow vehicle’s rear axle. Because of this, gooseneck hitches typically offer far greater towing stability relative to that of a truck and trailer connected by a bumper-pull-type hitch.

#155388. Tech Report: Cannabis customers develop psychosis years earlier, and the gap grows with age

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1626 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Cannabis customers develop psychosis years earlier, and the gap grows with age

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1626 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, A major international analysis has found that people who use cannabis experience their first episode of psychosis about two and a half years earlier, on average, than those who do not use the drug.
  • In a recent development, the findings, published in the journal Biological Psychiatry, come from researchers at UNSW Sydney.
  • Psychosis is a condition in which a person experiences a disruption in their perception of reality.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, A major international analysis has found that people who use cannabis experience their first episode of psychosis about two and a half years earlier, on average, than those who do not use the drug. Even more concerning, the difference becomes substantially larger with age, reaching more than six years among people who develop psychosis in their 30s or later.

In a recent development, the findings, published in the journal Biological Psychiatry, come from researchers at UNSW Sydney. They suggest that the potential psychiatric consequences of cannabis use may extend well beyond adolescence and could become more pronounced with prolonged exposure.

Psychosis is a condition in which a person experiences a disruption in their perception of reality. Symptoms can include hallucinations, false beliefs known as delusions, and disturbances in thinking or behavior. It can occur in schizophrenia and several other mental health disorders. Although psychosis most commonly begins during the late teenage years or early adulthood, it can develop at other stages of life. According to Psychosis Australia, up to 3% of adults will experience a diagnosed disorder involving psychosis during their lifetime.

Cannabis Linked to Earlier Psychosis Across Adulthood.

It has been revealed that to investigate the relationship between cannabis use and the timing of psychosis, researchers at UNSW Medicine analyzed 149 studies involving more than 71,000 participants. Most of the research had been conducted since 2011 in Europe, North America, and Australia, with the majority of studies focusing on people diagnosed with schizophrenia.

The researchers discovered that the difference in the age at which psychosis first appeared varied considerably across age groups.

In studies where the average age of psychosis onset was between 20 and 24, cannabis users experienced their first episode approximately 1.6 years earlier than non-users. That difference widened to 4.43 years in studies involving people whose psychosis emerged in their mid-to-late 20s (25-29).

The largest difference appeared in studies where psychosis developed at age 30 or later. In this group, cannabis owners experienced the condition an average of 6.3 years earlier than non-users.

These results suggest that the association between cannabis and earlier psychosis may become stronger as people grow older, potentially reflecting the effects of longer periods of cannabis exposure.

Why Cannabis Risks May Increase With Age.

Chief investigator Matthew Large, a psychiatrist and Conjoint Professor at UNSW's School of Clinical Medicine, mentioned the findings raise important questions about the long-term psychiatric effects of cannabis.

"We've tended to focus on the dangers of using cannabis in adolescence, when the brain is still developing, but the risk doesn't disappear once you're in your 20s," Prof. Large noted. "What we're seeing suggests a cumulative effect, where harm builds up over time, a bit like alcohol or nicotine.".

Interestingly, the analysis did not identify a statistically significant difference in the timing of psychosis between teenage cannabis users and teenagers who did not use cannabis.

According to recent reports, however, the researchers cautioned that this finding does not necessarily mean younger cannabis people face no risk. Psychosis rarely develops before the middle teenage years, leaving relatively little opportunity for its onset to shift to an even younger age.

In a recent development, "There may be a biological floor, in that there is only so much earlier that onset can be shifted. In younger groups, strong development, genetic or other psychosis risk factors may dominate, making any cannabis-related age shift harder to detect," Prof. Large mentioned.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers also stressed an important limitation. Because the analysis examined existing observational studies, it cannot establish that cannabis directly causes psychosis or makes the condition begin sooner. Demonstrating such a relationship experimentally would require research that deliberately exposed people to potential psychiatric harm, which would be unethical.

Industry observers note that nevertheless, Prof. Large believes the overall pattern provides meaningful evidence supporting a possible causal connection.

"But the consistency of the evidence, particularly the strong effect in older adults who likely have been using cannabis for longer, does support the theory that cannabis plays a causal role in the timing of psychosis onset, and possibly the onset of some cases among people who would not have otherwise developed psychosis.".

New Findings Challenge Assumptions About Cannabis After Age 25.

The latest research builds on two earlier investigations into cannabis use and the development of psychosis.

According to recent reports, in a smaller 2011 meta-analysis led by Prof. Large, researchers found that psychosis began approximately 2.7 years earlier among cannabis owners. A separate 2015 analysis reported that psychosis typically developed 6.3 years after cannabis use began.

However, neither earlier investigation had enough information to determine how the relationship differed across age groups.

By incorporating a much larger body of research, the newly introduced analysis allowed scientists to examine how the association changes across different stages of adulthood.

Lead author Carly Stevens, from UNSW's School of Biomedical Sciences, said the findings undermine the idea that avoiding cannabis during adolescence is sufficient to eliminate its potential psychiatric dangers.

"What we've found challenges the assumption that you'll be fine if you wait to smoke weed until your mid-20s; that's just not the case," Ms. Stevens remarked.

"There's been so much emphasis on adolescents not smoking cannabis, which is key, but we need to broaden the warnings for everyone.".

Why Even a Few Years of Delayed Psychosis Matter.

Although a difference of two or three years might initially seem relatively small, the researchers emphasized that the timing of psychosis can have profound consequences for a person's future.

In a recent development, the late teenage years and early adulthood are often periods when people complete their education, begin careers, establish relationships, and develop greater independence. Experiencing a serious psychiatric disorder earlier in life can interrupt these vital milestones.

Industry observers note that "People may miss out on study, job opportunities, travel, and relationships in those years, and treatment can come with physical side effects that can make life harder as well," Ms. Stevens said.

In a recent development, prof. Large emphasized the potential benefits of reducing or discontinuing cannabis use and the importance of delaying the onset of psychosis wherever possible.

It has been revealed that "It's a major illness, which robs you of your shared reality with family, friends and all those around you," he stated. "If we can delay psychosis by even a few years, people will be more likely to reach crucial milestones in education and training, and develop strong support networks, which can protect against psychosocial decline.".

According to recent reports, the potential benefits could also extend to healthcare systems. According to Prof. Large, psychotic disorders account for as much as 3% of health-related spending in developed countries. Preventing or delaying the onset of these conditions could therefore have substantial social and economic benefits.

Scientists Call for Stronger Cannabis Health Warnings.

Despite the inability to establish a direct cause-and-effect relationship, the researchers believe their findings provide sufficient justification for stronger warnings about the possible psychiatric consequences of cannabis use.

"We can't run direct experiments, so we have to go with the best evidence available," Prof. Large said. "In my view, the threshold for health warnings about cannabis and psychosis has definitely been met.".

It has been revealed that one concern is the growing popularity of medical cannabis. Prof. Large mentioned its increasing use as a therapeutic product may encourage some people to assume that it carries little risk.

He has also observed an increasing number of patients receiving treatment for psychosis who had previously been prescribed cannabis for medical conditions where evidence supporting its effectiveness remains limited.

"It's got this therapeutic halo around it, which blinds people to the risk.".

Industry observers note that another emerging concern involves cannabis edibles, which can contain elevated concentrations of Tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), the main compound responsible for the drug's mind altering effects. The availability of products containing higher THC concentrations raises additional questions about possible psychiatric risks.

In a recent development, at the same time, Prof. Large acknowledged that cannabis legalization could create opportunities to reduce harm, even though it would also make cannabis easier to obtain.

Legal regulation could allow governments to establish limits on product potency, improve consumer education, introduce taxation, and require buyers to receive clear information about potential health consequences.

Industry observers note that "You could tax it, regulate it, and require people to show they understand the risks before buying," Prof. Large stated.

More Research Needed on Long-Term Cannabis Exposure.

The researchers say further studies are necessary to understand the biological processes that might explain why the association between cannabis use and earlier psychosis becomes more pronounced with age.

In particular, they want to investigate whether repeated or prolonged cannabis exposure produces cumulative changes that influence when psychotic symptoms emerge.

They also recommend additional research focusing on older cannabis users, an increasingly important population as medical cannabis becomes more common and products containing high concentrations of THC become more widely available.

Another priority is improving how cannabis exposure is measured. The researchers argue that future studies need clearer and more consistent methods for recording cannabis consumption so that findings can be compared more reliably.

Ultimately, the new analysis highlights an crucial gap in public understanding of cannabis and mental health. While warnings have traditionally concentrated on teenage use, the findings suggest that potential psychiatric risks deserve attention throughout adulthood, particularly among people who continue using cannabis over many years.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that battlefield 6’s promised, season-extending patch has been officially detailed. The patch, version 1.1.3.5, arrives tomorrow, January 20 right when Season 1 was supposed to end. Part of the update’s goal is to extend the current season, until Season 2 kicks off in the middle of February.

Update 1.1.3.5 does, of course, have a change log of its own that goes beyond just the season’s extension, but the changes fall somewhere between not very exciting, and a bit puzzling.

Patch 1.1.3.5 is, for all intents and purposes, a smaller patch. When Battlefield Studios announced it earlier last week, the developer didn’t promise any major changes or fixes, so expectations never got out of hand.

Sources indicate that the patch is mainly made up of bug fixes, but it does have three key areas of improvements to gameplay. There’s a big focus on melee combat, how responsive/unresponsive it is with the various melee tools, and how melee behaviour interacts with sprinting and other animations.

Recent findings suggest that the end result should be faster attack speeds for the knife, and clearer wind-up animations for both the knife and the sledgehammer. The timing dictating when melee damage gets credited has also been made more consistent in different environments.

Industry observers note that interestingly, sprint is now only interrupted when the melee attack reaches its target. As it stands, sprinting is only interrupted after the full duration of the animation has been completed, which adds to the that perceived feeling of sluggishness.

According to recent reports, the other major, and arguably most confusing is the nerf to jet cannons. The patch is going to make jets far less stronger against other air vehicles, requiring 40% more hits to destroy a target. This is puzzling because jets - and air vehicles in general - are already the least survivable in Battlefield 6.

And, considering how the rest of a jet's arsenal is either situational or nearly ineffective, the cannons were really the one guaranteed way of downing other air vehicles, so long as you manage to land your shots consistently. While the change is wellmeaning, the percentage will likely be reduced in future patches.

Finally, the enhancement makes a few refinements to UI across the game, though mainly aimed at Redsec and modes where players wear armor. Armor bar visibility has been improved, and there’s a fix for the annoying bug that sometimes caused the armor bar to disappear every few seconds.

Avengers: Doomsday is now just around the corner and sees Simu Liu return as Shang-Chi for the first time in five years. The star, who last appeared in Shang-Chi and the Legend of the Ten Rings, will join the fight against Doctor Doom in the upcoming Marvel Phase 6 movie.

Not too much is known yet about his storyline in the upcoming movie, but we have seen a glimpse of his fight with Channing Tatum's Gambit in the trailer. Teasing the upcoming skirmish, Liu indicates they tried to make it as practical as they could.

It has been revealed that "To have a scene partner like Channing [Tatum], who is as insistent as I was about getting to do as much of it as possible, was critical to the success of that scene," Liu told Entertainment Weekly. "It was cool to have a dance partner who was as down to get into it as I was. There’s a lot of valid criticisms about the use of CGI in movies and everything, but for what it's worth, I think we really strived to make that sequence in particular as practical as it possibly could have been.".

This isn't the only fight scene that we've had an insight into ahead of Doomsday. A upcoming TV spot showing Magneto and Doom facing off on the battlefield as the iconic X-Men star tried to rip Doom's mask off his face. It's fair to say it didn't go to proposal.

#155385. Tech Report: Scientists discover a hidden gut defense that could prevent colon cancer
